title: Fundamentals — Optimization (Mid)
description: Optimization recognition at mid depth. 10 multi-question exercises (54 questions).

tasks.title: The Pipeline That Got Slower After the Schema Change

description.context: The NordGrid daily Silver pipeline has run in roughly 12 minutes for the past year. Two weeks ago, the team added a nullable struct field meta_audit to the Bronze meters schema (a small struct holding ingest_ts and source_file). The pipeline still produces correct output but now takes 38 minutes. Row counts and data volumes are unchanged. The Customer team's data engineer is asked to read the before-and-after physical plans and identify what changed.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: The NordGrid daily Silver pipeline has run in roughly 12 minutes for the past year. Two weeks ago, the team added a nullable struct field meta_audit to the Bronze meters schema (a small struct holding ingest_ts and source_file). The pipeline still produces correct output but now takes 38 minutes. Row counts and data volumes are unchanged. The Customer team's data engineer is asked to read the before-and-after physical plans and identify what changed.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: The Silver pipeline has an 8 AM SLA. At 38 minutes the pipeline still meets it but the margin is gone, and the on-call engineer has to babysit it whenever a downstream Bronze write runs late. The team lead has set a one-week deadline to find and fix the regression.

evidence.title: Platform context
evidence.content: Customer team OWNS the daily Silver pipeline; Platform team OWNS the Bronze ingestion that produces the schema. The schema change was shipped by the Platform team and signed off without consultation with the Customer team. Two other teams (Billing, Analytics) consume the Silver output but have not yet noticed the regression.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (1.2M-row Bronze table) plus a new nullable meta_audit struct field added 2026-04-26

evidence.label: Physical Plan Before
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
*(3) Project [meter_id, region, daily_kw_norm, daily_kw_grade]
+- *(3) Filter (daily_kw > 0.0)
   +- *(3) HashAggregate(keys=[meter_id, region, date], functions=[avg(daily_kw)])
      +- Exchange hashpartitioning(meter_id, region, date, 200)
         +- *(2) HashAggregate(keys=[meter_id, region, date], functions=[partial_avg(daily_kw)])
            +- *(2) Project [meter_id, region, date, daily_kw, daily_kw_norm, daily_kw_grade]
               +- *(2) BroadcastHashJoin [substation_id], [substation_id], LeftOuter, BuildRight
                  :- *(2) FileScan parquet meters [meter_id, region, date, daily_kw, substation_id]
                  +- BroadcastExchange HashedRelationBroadcastMode
                     +- *(1) FileScan parquet substations
WholeStageCodegen: 3 contiguous stages, all marked with the * prefix.

evidence.label: Physical Plan After
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
Project [meter_id, region, daily_kw_norm, daily_kw_grade]
+- Filter (daily_kw > 0.0)
   +- HashAggregate(keys=[meter_id, region, date], functions=[avg(daily_kw)])
      +- Exchange hashpartitioning(meter_id, region, date, 200)
         +- HashAggregate(keys=[meter_id, region, date], functions=[partial_avg(daily_kw)])
            +- Project [meter_id, region, date, daily_kw, daily_kw_norm, daily_kw_grade]
               +- BroadcastHashJoin [substation_id], [substation_id], LeftOuter, BuildRight
                  :- FileScan parquet meters [meter_id, region, date, daily_kw, substation_id, meta_audit]
                  +- BroadcastExchange HashedRelationBroadcastMode
                     +- FileScan parquet substations
WholeStageCodegen: NONE of the operators have the * prefix.

evidence.label: Runtime Metrics

fields.label: What is the proximate cause of the slowdown, as visible in the two physical plans?
options: The new meta_audit field added a struct column to the read schema, and reading struct columns is fundamentally slower than reading flat columns because the Parquet reader materialises each struct field by following pointer indirection on every row of the scan.

Whole-stage codegen has been disabled for every operator in the new plan, visible as the absence of the * prefix on the operators; the JVM falls back to the volcano-style row-iterator path which carries per-row method-dispatch cost across the pipeline.

The broadcast join is no longer being applied to the substations side, visible as the missing BroadcastHashJoin annotation in the physical plan above the meters scan; the join falls back to a sort-merge join whose shuffle cost dominates the runtime.

The exchange partition count increased from 200 to a much higher value because Catalyst sized the shuffle to the wider rows produced by the meta_audit struct, and the additional task dispatch overhead is what shows up in the new runtime.
fields.correctAnswer: Whole-stage codegen has been disabled for every operator in the new plan, visible as the absence of the * prefix on the operators; the JVM falls back to the volcano-style row-iterator path which carries per-row method-dispatch cost across the pipeline.
fields.rationale:
Comparing the two plans, the structural difference shows up in the prefixes: the before-plan marks operators with *, while the after-plan has none. The * marks operators inside a whole-stage codegen fused section. With every operator unfused, Spark runs the slower volcano-style iterator path, which is roughly 3x slower than codegen on CPU-bound transformations. The struct field's read cost (option A) is small. The broadcast join is still present. The shuffle partition count is unchanged at 200.

When this answer is wrong: If the after plan had shown a SortMergeJoin replacing the BroadcastHashJoin, option C's diagnosis would describe the dominant change. The exercise's framing (BroadcastHashJoin still present, just unfused) makes codegen fallback the right answer.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Picks the new struct field as the proximate cost, missing the codegen fallback that the field triggered.

Option C: Reaches for join-strategy regression that the plan does not actually show.

Option D: Invents a partition count change; the Exchange partition count is the same in both plans.

fields.label: Why does adding a nullable struct field disable whole-stage codegen for every operator in the chain?
options: Whole-stage codegen handles a fixed catalogue of types, and any new field added to a schema invalidates the codegen cache; the system rebuilds the generated code from scratch on the next run, which takes long enough on a 1.2M-row scan to dominate the runtime.

Whole-stage codegen requires the input row format to fit within a fixed JVM bytecode size limit, and adding a struct field grows the row template past the limit; the generated method exceeds the JVM's 8KB inlining heuristic and the engine falls back to row-by-row interpretation as a result.

Whole-stage codegen requires every projected column to appear in the fused operator chain at code-generation time, and including the meta_audit field in the read schema causes the field to be read but never referenced; the engine declines to fuse the chain when a read column has no consumer.

Whole-stage codegen handles flat primitive types; nested types like struct require a different code path, and adding any nested field to the read schema causes the engine to fall back to the non-codegen path for the whole-stage section that touches the read.
fields.correctAnswer: Whole-stage codegen handles flat primitive types; nested types like struct require a different code path, and adding any nested field to the read schema causes the engine to fall back to the non-codegen path for the whole-stage section that touches the read.
fields.rationale:
Whole-stage codegen handles a defined set of primitive types and operators. Nested types (struct, array, map) require a different code path, and the presence of any nested field in the section's input schema causes the codegen pass to skip fusion for that stage. The other options invent specific limits (cache invalidation, bytecode size, projection mismatch) that are not how codegen actually decides to fuse.

When this answer is wrong: If the meta_audit field had been added but immediately projected out before any other operator ran, codegen would have fused the rest of the chain because the nested field would not have appeared in the fused stage's input schema. The exercise's framing (struct present in the read schema) makes the fallback structural.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Invokes a codegen cache that does not work this way; codegen fallback for nested types is permanent, not a one-time invalidation.

Option B: Names a real but unrelated codegen limit (the 8KB inlining heuristic for very large fused stages); does not apply to a single struct addition.

Option C: Invents a 'no-consumer' rule; codegen does not require every read column to be consumed.

fields.label: Which fix in the pipeline code would restore whole-stage codegen without rolling back the schema change?
options: Add an explicit select on the meters DataFrame immediately after the read that lists only the flat columns the pipeline uses, dropping meta_audit from the projection so the codegen path sees only primitive types in the chain it would fuse together.

Replace the read of the partitioned meters Parquet with a read of a non-partitioned snapshot view that excludes the meta_audit field by table-level definition, restoring the schema shape the previous codegen pass used to compile the whole-stage operators.

Cache the meters DataFrame after the read so the codegen path runs once over the cached projection and the memory layout of the cache excludes the struct field; subsequent operations in the pipeline read from the cached form instead of the file.

Repartition the meters DataFrame after the read on the same key the join uses so Spark rewrites the layout in memory before the codegen pass runs over the operator chain, separating the read step from the fused stage above it.
fields.correctAnswer: Add an explicit select on the meters DataFrame immediately after the read that lists only the flat columns the pipeline uses, dropping meta_audit from the projection so the codegen path sees only primitive types in the chain it would fuse together.
fields.rationale:
Project the meta_audit field out as early as possible — a select with only the primitives, sitting just above the FileScan. The codegen pass over the operators downstream of the select sees only primitive types and fuses them as before. The other options chase plausible-looking workarounds (snapshot views, cache, repartition) that either change the table contract, add unnecessary cost, or do not address what blocks the codegen pass.

When this answer is wrong: If the pipeline genuinely needed the meta_audit field for a downstream operator (e.g., to filter on ingest_ts), the select-out fix would not preserve correctness and the team would have to design around the codegen-fallback cost. The exercise's framing (pipeline does not use meta_audit) makes the select-out clean.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Reaches for a snapshot view to dodge the schema; doable but more architectural than the proximate fix.

Option C: Invokes cache as a layout fix; cache exists for materialisation, not for codegen restoration.

Option D: Reorders steps without addressing the input-schema-to-codegen condition.

fields.label: The Customer team applies the fix and the pipeline drops to 14 minutes — close to the 12-minute baseline but not identical. Which residual cost likely accounts for the 2-minute gap?
options: The select that drops meta_audit adds a Project node above the FileScan that is itself outside the codegen-fused stage, contributing a small per-row overhead that compounds across 1.2M rows into a measurable but minor delta.

The Parquet reader still materialises the meta_audit field at the file level even though the projection drops it after the read, since the Parquet column index for nested fields requires reading the parent struct before the child field can be skipped.

The new schema increases the per-row size on disk slightly (the struct adds metadata even where the field is null), and the larger Parquet footer parse contributes additional time at scan setup that the previous schema did not pay.

Spark's plan caching layer carries a stale plan from before the fix shipped, and the first run after the fix recomputes the plan; subsequent runs would converge back to the 12-minute baseline as the plan cache warms up across iterations.
fields.correctAnswer: The new schema increases the per-row size on disk slightly (the struct adds metadata even where the field is null), and the larger Parquet footer parse contributes additional time at scan setup that the previous schema did not pay.
fields.rationale:
Even with the field projected out at execution time, the Parquet files themselves are slightly larger because the new schema writes struct metadata (offsets, null indicators) into each row group. The footer also lists more fields. Both contribute small constant overheads at read time. The other options invent specific cost paths (extra Project node cost, mandatory parent-struct read, plan caching) that either describe negligible costs or are factually wrong.

When this answer is wrong: If the original 12-minute baseline was measured with no meta_audit field at all (not just projected out), there would be no residual gap and the team would converge exactly to 12 minutes after a few runs. The exercise's framing (struct field permanently in the file) makes the read-side metadata the residual cost.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names a Project-node overhead that is essentially zero in codegen-fused chains.

Option B: Asserts mandatory parent-struct read for every nested column; not how Parquet's nested reader works.

Option D: Invokes a plan cache that does not behave this way; first-run cost is small.

fields.label: Looking at the runtime metrics, which observation would have pointed the engineer to the codegen-fallback diagnosis FIRST during the investigation?
options: Total runtime grew from 12 minutes to 38 minutes while data volume was unchanged; a roughly 3x slowdown without a corresponding workload change is the typical signature of a per-row code path change like codegen fallback rather than a data-volume change.

Executor CPU time grew from 11 minutes to 37 minutes, almost 1:1 with the wall-clock change; this rules out I/O regressions and shuffle regressions because both would inflate wall-clock time by more than CPU time, leaving CPU-path changes as the likely cause.

Stage count is identical at 4, which rules out plan changes like new shuffles; with the same DAG shape and the same data volume, a 3x slowdown in CPU time inside the existing operators is the codegen-fallback signature exactly.

Task dispatch overhead grew from ~200ms to ~12 seconds, a 60x jump that scales with task count; codegen fallback fragments a fused stage into many smaller operator-level tasks, and the dispatch overhead is the most distinctive numeric signature of the fragmentation.
fields.correctAnswer: Executor CPU time grew from 11 minutes to 37 minutes, almost 1:1 with the wall-clock change; this rules out I/O regressions and shuffle regressions because both would inflate wall-clock time by more than CPU time, leaving CPU-path changes as the likely cause.
fields.rationale:
The 1:1 growth between executor CPU time and wall-clock runtime is the distinctive signature. I/O slowdowns inflate wall-clock without inflating CPU time. Shuffle regressions also inflate wall-clock more than CPU. CPU time tracking wall-clock points at a per-row code path change, of which codegen fallback is the most common. The other options name observations that are true but less diagnostic; the CPU-vs-wall-clock ratio is what narrows the cause.

When this answer is wrong: If the regression had been caused by GC pressure (which inflates CPU but in a different signature — bursty rather than uniform), the same observation would point at GC rather than codegen and the engineer would need to look at GC time as a follow-up. The exercise's framing (uniform 3x growth in both CPU and wall-clock) points cleanly at codegen.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names runtime growth alone as the signature; growth is the symptom, not the diagnostic.

Option C: Stage count being unchanged is consistent with codegen fallback but is also consistent with many other causes; the CPU-time observation is more specific.

Option D: Names a real signal but a smaller one; codegen fallback does not necessarily fragment stages, and dispatch overhead at 12s is small relative to the 26-minute regression.

fields.label: What platform-level practice would have caught this regression before it reached production?
options: A pre-merge plan-stability check that captures the physical plan of each consumer pipeline against a representative input and flags when the codegen status of any operator changes between the previous and proposed Bronze schema versions during platform CI.

A pre-merge schema-fingerprint check that captures the column types of each consumer pipeline's read against the Bronze schema and flags when a nested type appears in a downstream pipeline's read for the first time across platform releases.

A pre-merge runtime regression test that runs each consumer pipeline against a representative input on the new and old schemas and flags when total runtime grows by more than a configured threshold across platform Bronze schema changes during CI checks.

A post-merge production canary that lets the new schema reach production on a 5% slice of the data, observes consumer pipeline runtimes for a settling period, and rolls back the schema when any consumer runtime grows beyond its SLA tolerance during the canary window.
fields.correctAnswer: A post-merge production canary that lets the new schema reach production on a 5% slice of the data, observes consumer pipeline runtimes for a settling period, and rolls back the schema when any consumer runtime grows beyond its SLA tolerance during the canary window.
fields.rationale:
Plan-stability checks (option A) are powerful but expensive at platform scale and require representative inputs that match each consumer's pattern. Schema-fingerprint checks (option B) catch the schema-level change but do not catch the runtime impact. Pre-merge runtime regression tests (option C) are slow to run and produce false positives. A post-merge canary on a small data slice catches the regression where it matters (in production) at low cost, with rollback as the safety net. The senior pattern: optimisation regressions are detected most cheaply in production canaries with rollback, not in CI.

When this answer is wrong: On platforms where rollback is operationally costly (e.g., schemas that change downstream contracts in ways that cannot be reverted), pre-merge plan-stability checks (option A) are the right pattern even at their higher cost. The exercise's framing (Bronze schema additions can be rolled back) makes the canary the cheaper option.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Picks the most thorough check; correct for some platforms but expensive for routine schema additions.

Option B: Catches schema change but misses runtime impact; a half-measure.

Option C: Picks pre-merge regression tests; slow and noisy at platform scale.

tasks.title: Two Plans, One Query

description.context: A NordGrid analytics engineer runs the same query twice — once on Monday and again on Friday after a data engineering teammate ran ANALYZE TABLE on the meters and substations tables on Wednesday. The query is identical in both cases. The plans differ. The teammate asks the engineer to read both plans, identify which one is the post-ANALYZE plan, and explain why the change happened.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid analytics engineer runs the same query twice — once on Monday and again on Friday after a data engineering teammate ran ANALYZE TABLE on the meters and substations tables on Wednesday. The query is identical in both cases. The plans differ. The teammate asks the engineer to read both plans, identify which one is the post-ANALYZE plan, and explain why the change happened.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: The Friday plan finishes in 4 minutes. The Monday plan finished in 23 minutes. Both produced the same results. The team is trying to decide whether to add ANALYZE to the daily pipeline schedule, and the engineer's interpretation of the plan delta is what the decision rests on.

evidence.title: Platform context
evidence.content: The Customer team OWNS the meters table; the Substations team OWNS the substations table. ANALYZE has not historically been part of either team's pipeline schedule. The Analytics team consumes both tables and is the one currently feeling the cost of stale statistics on join planning.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (1.2M rows), substations.csv (200 rows for the 12-region NordGrid expansion)

evidence.label: Query
evidence.content:
result = (
    spark.table('nordgrid.meters')
        .filter(col('date') == '2026-05-08')
        .join(spark.table('nordgrid.substations'), 'substation_id', 'left')
        .groupBy('region')
        .agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total_kw'))
)

evidence.label: Plan X
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
HashAggregate(keys=[region], functions=[sum(daily_kw)])
+- Exchange hashpartitioning(region, 200)
   +- HashAggregate(keys=[region], functions=[partial_sum(daily_kw)])
      +- Project [region, daily_kw]
         +- SortMergeJoin [substation_id], [substation_id], LeftOuter
            :- Sort [substation_id]
            :  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(substation_id, 200)
            :     +- Filter (date = 2026-05-08)
            :        +- FileScan parquet meters
            +- Sort [substation_id]
               +- Exchange hashpartitioning(substation_id, 200)
                  +- FileScan parquet substations
Statistics: meters [sizeInBytes=8.0 EiB (default fallback)], substations [sizeInBytes=8.0 EiB (default fallback)]

evidence.label: Plan Y
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
HashAggregate(keys=[region], functions=[sum(daily_kw)])
+- Exchange hashpartitioning(region, 200)
   +- HashAggregate(keys=[region], functions=[partial_sum(daily_kw)])
      +- Project [region, daily_kw]
         +- BroadcastHashJoin [substation_id], [substation_id], LeftOuter, BuildRight
            :- Filter (date = 2026-05-08)
            :  +- FileScan parquet meters
            +- BroadcastExchange HashedRelationBroadcastMode
               +- FileScan parquet substations
Statistics: meters [sizeInBytes=42 GB], substations [sizeInBytes=18 KB]

fields.label: Which plan is the post-ANALYZE plan, and what is the visible signal that distinguishes it?
options: Plan Y is the post-ANALYZE plan; the Statistics line shows real byte sizes for both tables (42 GB and 18 KB) instead of the 8.0 EiB default-fallback value, and the join strategy switched from sort-merge to broadcast as a result of the size knowledge.

Plan X is the post-ANALYZE plan; the post-ANALYZE planner runs a more conservative strategy by default and falls back to sort-merge when the statistics indicate that broadcasting either side might exceed the broadcast threshold under any pessimistic estimate the planner produces.

Plan Y is the post-ANALYZE plan; the partition count on the Exchange node dropped from 200 to a smaller value because the post-ANALYZE planner chose a tighter shuffle granularity matching the post-aggregate row count it estimated from the new statistics.

Plan X is the post-ANALYZE plan; the absence of a BroadcastExchange in plan X reflects the post-ANALYZE planner explicitly choosing to avoid broadcast in favor of sort-merge for tables whose statistics show wide row distributions across the join key.
fields.correctAnswer: Plan Y is the post-ANALYZE plan; the Statistics line shows real byte sizes for both tables (42 GB and 18 KB) instead of the 8.0 EiB default-fallback value, and the join strategy switched from sort-merge to broadcast as a result of the size knowledge.
fields.rationale:
The Statistics annotation tells the story: plan Y reports concrete sizes (42 GB and 18 KB), while plan X reports 8.0 EiB on both sides — Spark's default fallback when ANALYZE has never produced real statistics. With real numbers, the substations side comes in well under the broadcast threshold and the planner picks BroadcastHashJoin. The other options either invert which plan is post-ANALYZE or invent specific behaviors (conservative strategy, partition count change, broadcast avoidance) that the plans do not show.

When this answer is wrong: If the broadcast threshold had been set below 18 KB (an unusual configuration), the post-ANALYZE plan would still pick sort-merge because the substations side would not qualify for broadcast even with real statistics. The exercise's framing (default broadcast threshold of 10 MB) makes the size knowledge sufficient.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Inverts which plan is post-ANALYZE and invents a 'conservative strategy' default.

Option C: Picks the right plan but for the wrong reason (partition count change that the plans do not show).

Option D: Inverts which plan is post-ANALYZE and invents a row-distribution criterion.

fields.label: Why did the Monday plan use SortMergeJoin instead of BroadcastHashJoin even though the substations table is only 18 KB?
options: Without ANALYZE statistics, Spark's planner reads only the Parquet footer for size estimation and the footer for the substations table reports only the row count, not the byte size, leaving the planner without the input it needs to decide on broadcast for the join's build side.

Without ANALYZE statistics, Spark falls back to a default size estimate of 8 EiB for tables whose statistics have not been collected; the 8 EiB is much larger than the broadcast threshold (default 10 MB) so neither side qualifies for broadcast on the join planning step.

Without ANALYZE statistics, Spark's planner uses cardinality estimates that propagate inflated row counts through the join graph; the estimated post-filter cardinality of the meters table appeared larger than either side's broadcast eligibility could accommodate.

Without ANALYZE statistics, the broadcast eligibility check requires manual hints in the query; the absence of a broadcast hint in this query made the planner pick sort-merge as the default join strategy across the whole table catalog.
fields.correctAnswer: Without ANALYZE statistics, Spark falls back to a default size estimate of 8 EiB for tables whose statistics have not been collected; the 8 EiB is much larger than the broadcast threshold (default 10 MB) so neither side qualifies for broadcast on the join planning step.
fields.rationale:
The 8.0 EiB on the Statistics line is Spark's fallback when no real statistics exist. The fallback value is intentionally larger than any conceivable broadcast threshold (default 10 MB) so the planner always picks the safer sort-merge when statistics are unknown. Footer-based sizing (option A) is partially used but does not save the broadcast decision here. Cardinality-estimate propagation (option C) plays a role for filter pushdown but not for broadcast decisions. Manual hints (option D) are not required; the planner can choose broadcast on its own when statistics support it.

When this answer is wrong: If Spark were configured with a lower default fallback (e.g., the cost-based optimiser configured to fall back to footer-derived sizes), option A's mechanism would describe the actual planning step. The exercise's framing (default fallback to 8 EiB) makes the broadcast threshold the deciding criterion.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names a partial mechanism (footer-based sizing) without naming the 8 EiB fallback that overrides it.

Option C: Conflates row-count estimation with broadcast eligibility; broadcast uses byte-size.

Option D: Asserts that broadcast requires a hint; it does not when statistics support it.

fields.label: The team considers adding ANALYZE to the daily pipeline. Which alternative gives most of the same benefit without paying the per-day ANALYZE cost?
options: Increase the broadcast threshold (spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold) to a much higher value so the planner accepts broadcasts up to that size; the planner picks broadcast when even the pessimistic 8 EiB default falls under the new ceiling.

Add a broadcast hint to the substations side of the join in the team's queries (or query templates); the hint instructs the planner to broadcast that side regardless of statistics, achieving the same outcome the post-ANALYZE plan reached on its own.

Enable AQE so the planner can reconvert the join to broadcast at runtime once the actual filtered row count is known; the post-shuffle conversion gives the same broadcast outcome as ANALYZE but driven by runtime evidence rather than pre-collected statistics.

Run ANALYZE only on the rarely-changing reference tables (substations, tariffs) and skip it for the meters table; the reference-table statistics are the binding input for join-strategy decisions and the meters table's statistics are less load-bearing.
fields.correctAnswer: Enable AQE so the planner can reconvert the join to broadcast at runtime once the actual filtered row count is known; the post-shuffle conversion gives the same broadcast outcome as ANALYZE but driven by runtime evidence rather than pre-collected statistics.
fields.rationale:
AQE's runtime adjustment is exactly the alternative path. The first stage (the post-filter Exchange on the meters side) runs to completion, AQE observes the actual data sizes, and if either side now fits the broadcast threshold the planner re-plans the join. This achieves the same broadcast outcome ANALYZE provides without per-day collection cost. Raising the broadcast threshold to swallow 8 EiB (option A) would broadcast everything including the 42 GB meters table. Manual hints (option B) work but require touching every query. Selective ANALYZE (option D) is good practice but still costs collection time.

When this answer is wrong: If AQE is disabled in the cluster's default configuration (some legacy clusters do this), option B's manual hints become the right answer because runtime replanning is unavailable. The exercise's framing (AQE available) makes it the cleanest alternative.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Raises the broadcast threshold to absurd values to defeat the 8 EiB fallback; would broadcast huge tables.

Option B: Picks manual hints; works but requires per-query maintenance.

Option D: Picks selective ANALYZE; still requires a collection schedule.

fields.label: If the team adopts AQE instead of ANALYZE, the Monday plan would still START as a SortMergeJoin. What changes at runtime?
options: AQE inspects the size of the post-Exchange data on each side of the join after the first stage runs and triggers a re-plan that converts the operator to a sort-merge join with skew handling, which is more efficient than the original sort-merge for skewed substation_id distributions.

AQE collapses the two Exchange nodes feeding the SortMergeJoin into a single Exchange after observing that both sides hash-partition on the same key, removing one shuffle from the plan and reducing the runtime by approximately the cost of one shuffle's I/O.

AQE inspects the size of the actual data flowing into the join after the first stage runs; when the substations side after its Exchange shows up as 18 KB it falls under the broadcast threshold, and AQE replans the join to BroadcastHashJoin for the remainder of the query.

AQE rewrites the SortMergeJoin into a BroadcastHashJoin during query compilation by reading the runtime statistics of any earlier execution of the same query against the same tables, using a session-level cache keyed on the query plan signature for cross-query reuse.
fields.correctAnswer: AQE rewrites the SortMergeJoin into a BroadcastHashJoin during query compilation by reading the runtime statistics of any earlier execution of the same query against the same tables, using a session-level cache keyed on the query plan signature for cross-query reuse.
fields.rationale:
AQE re-plans the join only AFTER the first stage of the query has run. AQE's broadcast conversion is a runtime decision, not a compile-time one — it inspects materialised post-Exchange data sizes and re-plans the remaining stages. The exercise's framing (AQE replans the join to BroadcastHashJoin) describes the actual mechanism. Skew handling (option A) is a different AQE feature. Exchange collapsing (option B) is not an AQE mechanism. The session-level plan cache (option D) is what option D claims and is wrong because AQE replans based on RUNTIME data, not on cached prior runs.

When this answer is wrong: If the substations side after its Exchange exceeded the broadcast threshold (e.g., due to a large reference table), AQE would not convert and the SortMergeJoin would run to completion. The exercise's framing (substations is genuinely small) makes the conversion fire.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names skew handling, a different AQE feature, instead of broadcast conversion.

Option B: Invents an Exchange-collapsing AQE feature that does not exist.

Option C: Names the right outcome but with a true description; this is the answer that is correct, not D.

fields.label: Which observation in the runtime metrics would have flagged the stale-statistics problem to a passing reviewer of the Monday run?
options: The plan reports sizeInBytes of 8.0 EiB for the substations table — a magnitude orders larger than the file system actually holds; the EiB default-fallback value is the diagnostic signature that ANALYZE has never run on the table or has not run since a structural change.

The Exchange node's actual shuffle write byte count would have been visible in the SQL UI after the first stage; comparing the actual byte count to the planner's estimated row count would have revealed the order-of-magnitude estimation error that drove the plan choice.

When this answer is wrong: If a reviewer is doing a post-mortem after the Monday run finished, the runtime observations (option D's Exchange write size, option C's task histogram) become the more direct diagnostic because the EiB value is buried in the plan output. The exercise's framing (passing reviewer of the Monday run) makes the plan-level signature the first thing visible.

tasks.title: When 200 Shuffle Partitions Is the Wrong Answer

description.context: A NordGrid data engineer is tuning a daily aggregation that groups 1.2M rows of meter readings by region and date. The query runs on a 24-core cluster (3 executors × 8 cores) with the default spark.sql.shuffle.partitions set to 200. Per-task durations show p50 at 2.1 seconds and p99 at 4.0 seconds; total stage time is 8 minutes. The engineer suspects the partition count is wrong and wants to evaluate four candidate counts: 16, 48, 200, and 600.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid data engineer is tuning a daily aggregation that groups 1.2M rows of meter readings by region and date. The query runs on a 24-core cluster (3 executors × 8 cores) with the default spark.sql.shuffle.partitions set to 200. Per-task durations show p50 at 2.1 seconds and p99 at 4.0 seconds; total stage time is 8 minutes. The engineer suspects the partition count is wrong and wants to evaluate four candidate counts: 16, 48, 200, and 600.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: The aggregation runs every 30 minutes against the latest hour's readings. Total wall-clock budget for the aggregation is 90 seconds. At 8 minutes the budget is exceeded by 5x, and the engineer needs a count that fits the cluster shape and the workload size.

evidence.title: Platform context
evidence.content: The Customer team OWNS this aggregation. The cluster is shared with the Billing team's nightly invoice job (which uses 600 shuffle partitions for its 50M-row workload) and the Analytics team's ad-hoc queries (which set 32 partitions per query). The team is debating whether to set the configuration globally or per-job.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (1.2M rows for the latest hour's readings)

evidence.title: Cluster Spec
evidence.content: 3 executors × 8 cores = 24 task slots; 32 GB RAM per executor; 1.2M rows × ~250 bytes = ~300 MB pre-shuffle

evidence.title: Current Config
evidence.content: spark.sql.shuffle.partitions = 200 (cluster default)

evidence.label: Per Task Metrics At 200

fields.label: What is wrong with the current 200-partition configuration for this workload?
options: 200 partitions is below the cluster's available task slots and the executors run idle for most of the stage; the planner should have set it to 24 (one partition per slot) to keep all task slots active and remove the per-stage idle gap that drives the runtime up to 8 minutes.

200 partitions creates too much per-task scheduler overhead because Spark dispatches each partition individually and the dispatch cost grows linearly with the partition count; the dispatch cost dominates the per-stage time when partitions are smaller than ~1 MB each in size.

200 partitions on 24 task slots forces 8-9 wave rounds of task execution on the cluster; with only ~300 MB of data pre-shuffle, each task processes about 1.5 MB which is too small to amortise the per-task setup cost across the work each task does.

200 partitions exceeds the cluster's network throughput limit because each partition triggers an inter-executor data transfer; the limit caps the effective partition processing rate at about 24 partitions per second across the three executors of the cluster setup.
fields.correctAnswer: 200 partitions on 24 task slots forces 8-9 wave rounds of task execution on the cluster; with only ~300 MB of data pre-shuffle, each task processes about 1.5 MB which is too small to amortise the per-task setup cost across the work each task does.
fields.rationale:
On 24 task slots, 200 partitions means roughly 8-9 waves of execution. With 300 MB of data, each task processes only 1.5 MB. Per-task setup cost (task dispatch, executor handoff, partition open) is roughly fixed at 50-100 ms; processing 1.5 MB worth of work at that cost is poor amortisation. The other options invent mechanisms (idle slots from too few partitions, scheduler dispatch as the bottleneck, network throughput cap) that are not the proximate cost.

When this answer is wrong: If the per-row processing cost were much higher (e.g., a heavy UDF), 200 partitions could be the right count even at 1.5 MB per task because the per-task processing time would dwarf the setup cost. The exercise's framing (simple aggregation) makes setup-cost amortisation the binding factor.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Inverts the diagnosis; 200 partitions is too many, not too few.

Option B: Reaches for scheduler dispatch as the dominant cost; dispatch is small compared to per-task setup at this scale.

Option D: Invents a network throughput cap; not how Spark's shuffle scheduling works.

fields.label: Of the four candidates (16, 48, 200, 600), which is the best fit for this workload?
options: 48 partitions is the best fit; it gives 2 partitions per task slot, which keeps all 24 slots busy across roughly 2 waves while keeping per-task data large enough to amortise the per-task setup cost across roughly 6-7 MB of data per task.

16 partitions is the best fit; with 24 task slots available and 16 partitions to process, the stage runs in a single wave with no dispatch overhead, and each task processes about 19 MB which is in the comfortable per-task range for short tasks on this kind of aggregate workload.

600 partitions is the best fit; with more partitions the planner has more freedom to balance keys across tasks and the workload's distribution across regions and dates fits the larger partition count more cleanly than the smaller candidates the team considered first.

200 partitions is the best fit at this data size; the default exists because it works for most workloads, and the per-task time of 2 seconds is a reasonable target that balances setup overhead with task granularity for the 24-core cluster shape.
fields.correctAnswer: 48 partitions is the best fit; it gives 2 partitions per task slot, which keeps all 24 slots busy across roughly 2 waves while keeping per-task data large enough to amortise the per-task setup cost across roughly 6-7 MB of data per task.
fields.rationale:
Two waves on 24 slots means 48 partitions. Each task processes ~6.25 MB, which is comfortable for the per-task setup amortisation. 16 partitions is too few — the stage runs in less than a wave on 24 slots, leaving 8 slots idle. 600 perpetuates the 200-partitions problem at a worse ratio. 200 is the current configuration; staying with it does not solve anything.

When this answer is wrong: If the cluster were 48 cores instead of 24, the same workload would point to 96 partitions for the two-wave target. The exercise's framing (24-core cluster) makes 48 the right size.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Picks single-wave processing; leaves 8 slots idle and offers no margin for skew.

Option C: Picks Billing's count without checking workload-cluster fit; 600 is right for Billing's larger workload.

Option D: Picks the default; defaults are starting points, not answers for tuned workloads.

fields.label: The engineer notices that the Billing team uses 600 partitions for their 50M-row workload. Why does 600 work for Billing but not for this 1.2M-row job?
options: Billing's 50M-row workload has higher per-row processing cost because it computes invoices that involve a join with tariff tables and a per-row evaluation of pricing rules; the higher per-row cost makes a smaller per-task partition appropriate even at 600 total partitions.

Billing's 50M-row workload uses a different aggregation function (collect_list) that is sensitive to memory pressure per task; smaller per-task data through 600 partitions reduces the chance of any one task spilling its collect_list buffer to disk during the run.

Billing's 50M-row workload runs on a different cluster with 96 cores instead of 24 cores; 600 partitions gives the larger cluster about 6 waves of work which fits its task slot count, while 600 on this 24-core cluster would multiply the wave count to 25.

Billing's 50M-row workload is shuffle-heavy at scale; 600 partitions keeps each per-task partition around 80 MB, which is in the right range for a workload of that size and the same range the 1.2M-row workload would target with 48 partitions on this cluster.
fields.correctAnswer: Billing's 50M-row workload is shuffle-heavy at scale; 600 partitions keeps each per-task partition around 80 MB, which is in the right range for a workload of that size and the same range the 1.2M-row workload would target with 48 partitions on this cluster.
fields.rationale:
The right way to size partitions is to target a per-task data range (commonly 50-200 MB for shuffle-heavy work). Billing's 50 GB ÷ 600 ≈ 83 MB per task; this workload at 300 MB ÷ 48 ≈ 6 MB per task. The same target range produces different counts because the data sizes differ by 100x. The other options invoke specific differences (per-row cost, aggregation function, cluster size) that are plausible but not the structural reason.

When this answer is wrong: If both teams ran on the same cluster but the data sizes were comparable, the partition-count difference would point at a specific workload property (skew, aggregation function, etc.) rather than at data-size scaling. The exercise's framing (workload sizes differ by 40x) makes the data-size-driven sizing the structural answer.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Reaches for per-row cost as the structural reason; cost matters but data-size scaling is structural.

Option B: Picks aggregation function specifics; collect_list is unusual and not the structural reason.

Option C: Names cluster-size differences; possible but the question framing implies same-cluster context.

fields.label: The team decides to set partition counts per-job rather than globally. Which mechanism is the right tool?
options: Set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions in the cluster's spark-defaults.conf to a workload-appropriate value across the cluster; per-job tuning happens through job-level overrides that the cluster's runtime resolves at submit time before the job starts executing.

Use spark.conf.set('spark.sql.shuffle.partitions', N) at the top of each job; the setting takes effect for all subsequent shuffles in that SparkSession and does not affect other jobs running concurrently against the same cluster's resource pool.

Use repartition(N) on the DataFrame before each shuffle-triggering operation; repartition is the explicit per-stage knob that overrides the session-level setting for the specific shuffle the engineer is trying to size.

Enable AQE and rely on coalesce-shuffle-partitions to size each shuffle automatically based on the actual data volumes at runtime; AQE replaces the per-job tuning with adaptive sizing that fits each shuffle to its observed input data.
fields.correctAnswer: Use spark.conf.set('spark.sql.shuffle.partitions', N) at the top of each job; the setting takes effect for all subsequent shuffles in that SparkSession and does not affect other jobs running concurrently against the same cluster's resource pool.
fields.rationale:
Per-job partition tuning belongs at the SparkSession level and spark.conf.set is the right knob. The setting takes effect for all subsequent shuffle operations in the session without affecting concurrent jobs. Cluster-level defaults (option A) apply globally and are not per-job. repartition (option C) reshapes the data but does not configure shuffles that come from groupBy or join. AQE coalesce (option D) is automatic but is a different lever — useful, but not the answer to 'how do we set partitions per-job'.

When this answer is wrong: If the team wants to override partition count for a specific shuffle in the middle of a job (rather than for all shuffles in the session), repartition (option C) is the right tool. The exercise's framing (per-job, not per-stage) makes the session-level set the answer.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Picks cluster-level configuration; not per-job.

Option C: Confuses repartition (data redistribution) with shuffle partition count.

Option D: Picks AQE as a substitute; useful complement but not the per-job partition knob.

fields.label: After setting partitions to 48 the stage drops to 75 seconds. Which observation would confirm the choice was right (rather than coincidentally faster)?
options: Total stage time at 75 seconds is below the 90-second SLA; SLA conformance is the team's contract with downstream consumers and is the right success criterion regardless of which intermediate metrics moved between the two configurations.

Per-task duration histogram now shows p50 at 5-7 seconds and p99 at 10-12 seconds; the histogram shifted into a range where setup cost is small relative to processing time and where the spread between p50 and p99 indicates a healthy load distribution across tasks.

Task slot utilization in the cluster's Spark UI shows steady occupation at near-100% across the stage's duration with no idle gaps between waves; consistent slot utilization is the signature that the partition count matches the cluster shape correctly.

Shuffle write byte count remained the same at ~300 MB total; data volume invariance across the partition-count change confirms the workload itself did not change, so the time difference reflects partition count effects rather than other run-to-run variation.
fields.correctAnswer: Task slot utilization in the cluster's Spark UI shows steady occupation at near-100% across the stage's duration with no idle gaps between waves; consistent slot utilization is the signature that the partition count matches the cluster shape correctly.
fields.rationale:
What the team is trying to achieve with partition tuning is full executor occupancy; if the SQL UI shows the slots filled the whole way through, the count fits the cluster. SLA conformance (option A) is necessary but not sufficient — the run could be coincidentally fast. Task duration histogram (option B) is informative but secondary. Shuffle write byte invariance (option D) only confirms the data did not change, not that the partition choice was right. Slot utilization is what the partition tuning is trying to achieve.

When this answer is wrong: If the cluster were autoscaling and the slot count varied during the stage, slot utilization would be misleading and the per-task duration histogram (option B) would be the more reliable signal. The exercise's framing (fixed 24-slot cluster) makes utilization the cleanest signal.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names the contractual outcome (SLA met) without confirming the mechanism (partition fit).

Option B: Names a useful but secondary signal; histograms confirm distribution, utilization confirms fit.

Option D: Names an invariance check that controls for confounders but does not confirm fit.

fields.label: A teammate asks 'Why don't we just always set partitions = number of cores?' What is the strongest argument against this rule?
options: Setting partitions equal to core count assumes the workload fits in a single wave on the cluster; for workloads larger than the cluster can hold in memory at once, single-wave processing leads to spill or OOM, and multiple waves with smaller per-task data are the safer choice.

Setting partitions equal to core count ignores the variability in per-task duration; one slow task in a single-wave configuration leaves all other slots idle while it finishes, while two waves of half-size tasks would have given the cluster a chance to redistribute the slow keys.

Setting partitions equal to core count works only when key cardinality is at least equal to core count; for an aggregation grouping by region (cardinality 12) on a 24-core cluster, the planner cannot create 24 non-empty partitions and 12 cores stay idle for the stage.

Setting partitions equal to core count produces zero idle time but also zero margin for failure recovery; if any task fails and needs retry, the failed task must run on its original slot in serial with the remaining work, blocking the stage from completing on time.
fields.correctAnswer: Setting partitions equal to core count assumes the workload fits in a single wave on the cluster; for workloads larger than the cluster can hold in memory at once, single-wave processing leads to spill or OOM, and multiple waves with smaller per-task data are the safer choice.
fields.rationale:
The rule presumes that everything fits into memory simultaneously across all executors. For workloads larger than aggregate executor memory, single-wave runs would spill or OOM. Multiple waves are the safety mechanism. The other options name real but smaller concerns (slow-task tail effect, key-cardinality limits, retry margin) that matter in specific cases but are not the structural reason for the rule's failure.

When this answer is wrong: If the workload genuinely fits in cluster memory across all task slots simultaneously (a small workload), partitions = cores can be the right configuration and option B's slow-task argument becomes the strongest remaining concern. The exercise's framing (no fit assumption) makes the OOM risk the structural argument.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Names slow-task tail; real concern but smaller than memory-fit risk.

Option C: Names key-cardinality limits; specific edge case, not the general rule's failure.

Option D: Names retry margin; relevant for resilience, not for the basic rule.

tasks.title: repartition or coalesce Before the Write

description.context: A NordGrid pipeline produces a Gold table holding daily per-region summaries — about 12 rows per day across 12 regions. The pipeline reads 1.2M Silver rows, aggregates them, and writes the result. The output currently produces 200 small Parquet files (one per shuffle partition, most files holding zero or one row). The downstream consumer is a small dashboard that does spark.read.parquet over the Gold directory and complains about the file count. The engineer is considering repartition(12), coalesce(12), repartition(1), and coalesce(1) before the write.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid pipeline produces a Gold table holding daily per-region summaries — about 12 rows per day across 12 regions. The pipeline reads 1.2M Silver rows, aggregates them, and writes the result. The output currently produces 200 small Parquet files (one per shuffle partition, most files holding zero or one row). The downstream consumer is a small dashboard that does spark.read.parquet over the Gold directory and complains about the file count. The engineer is considering repartition(12), coalesce(12), repartition(1), and coalesce(1) before the write.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: The dashboard reads the Gold table every 5 minutes. Each read pays the per-file open cost across 200 files. The Gold writer runs nightly. The engineer wants to fix the file count without breaking either the writer's performance or the readers' parallelism.

evidence.title: Platform context
evidence.content: The Customer team OWNS the Gold writer. The Analytics team OWNS the dashboard. Three other teams (Billing, Substations, Finance) read the Gold table once per day in batch jobs that are not file-count-sensitive. The dashboard's 5-minute polling makes it the dominant read consumer.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (Silver source, 1.2M rows; Gold output, ~12 rows per day across 12 regions)

evidence.title: Current Writer Chain
evidence.content:
(silver
    .groupBy('region', 'date')
    .agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total_kw'))
    .write.mode('overwrite')
    .parquet('s3://nordgrid/gold/regional_daily/'))

evidence.title: Current Output
evidence.content: 200 Parquet files, average size 80 bytes, total 16 KB on disk

evidence.label: Candidate Edits
evidence.content:
[
  "Add .repartition(12) before .write — produces 12 files via a hash-shuffle on no key (round-robin)",
  "Add .coalesce(12) before .write — produces 12 files by merging the 200 post-aggregate partitions",
  "Add .repartition(1) before .write — produces 1 file via a hash-shuffle to a single partition",
  "Add .coalesce(1) before .write — produces 1 file by collapsing all partitions into one"
]

fields.label: What is the proximate cause of the 200-file output?
options: The default spark.sql.shuffle.partitions of 200 sets the post-aggregate partition count, and each of the 200 partitions writes its own Parquet file regardless of how few rows the partition contains; the writer creates a file per partition unconditionally.

The default writer behavior is to produce one file per executor task slot and the cluster has 200 slots configured; each slot opens its own writer for the assigned partition, producing one file per slot at the write boundary of the pipeline.

The Parquet writer splits each partition into multiple files by default to fit the configured maxRecordsPerFile bound, and 200 files reflects the 12 post-aggregate rows being distributed across the writer's default file-count strategy.

The aggregate produces 200 partitions because Catalyst inserts an Exchange with 200 partitions before the HashAggregate, and the post-aggregate partition count carries through to the writer; each non-empty partition produces a file at write time.
fields.correctAnswer: The aggregate produces 200 partitions because Catalyst inserts an Exchange with 200 partitions before the HashAggregate, and the post-aggregate partition count carries through to the writer; each non-empty partition produces a file at write time.
fields.rationale:
GroupBy triggers a shuffle whose partition count is set by spark.sql.shuffle.partitions. The post-aggregate stage carries that partition count into the writer, and each non-empty partition produces a file. With 12 output rows and 200 partitions, only 12 partitions are non-empty (and a few may have multiple rows due to hash collisions), explaining why the count appears around 200 files. Option A states the same outcome but credits the writer rather than the upstream Exchange; both are partial truths, but D is more precise about the mechanism.

When this answer is wrong: If the team had explicitly set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to a different value before the aggregate, the file count would track that value. The exercise's framing (default 200) makes the upstream Exchange the structural source.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names the right outcome but pins it on writer behavior rather than the upstream shuffle that creates the partitions.

Option B: Conflates executor task slots with shuffle partitions; they are independent.

Option C: Reaches for maxRecordsPerFile as a per-file split mechanism; would explain MORE files per partition, not 200 sparse partitions.

fields.label: Which candidate is the right edit for this workload?
options: repartition(12) is the right edit; the round-robin shuffle distributes the 12 output rows evenly across 12 files at one row per file, and the explicit shuffle gives Catalyst a chance to optimize across the boundary it introduces.

coalesce(12) is the right edit; it produces 12 files by merging the 200 post-aggregate partitions without an extra shuffle, and the small post-aggregate row count means the merge cost is negligible compared to a full shuffle.

repartition(1) is the right edit; with only 12 output rows there is no benefit to multiple files, and a single file is the simplest layout for the dashboard's polling read on the Gold table directory.

coalesce(1) is the right edit; collapsing all partitions into one avoids a shuffle and produces a single file, which is the most efficient possible layout for the 12-row Gold output that the dashboard reads.
fields.correctAnswer: coalesce(12) is the right edit; it produces 12 files by merging the 200 post-aggregate partitions without an extra shuffle, and the small post-aggregate row count means the merge cost is negligible compared to a full shuffle.
fields.rationale:
Of the four candidates, the no-shuffle reduction to twelve files is the right structural fit: there is no expensive redistribution step, and the resulting file count matches the row count. repartition(12) does the same but adds a shuffle that costs more than it saves. coalesce(1) and repartition(1) both produce a single file, which is unnecessarily restrictive for downstream parallelism even at this row count.

When this answer is wrong: If the row count were much higher (say, 12,000 instead of 12) and the partitions were unevenly distributed, repartition(12) would be the right choice because the round-robin redistribution evens out the file sizes. The exercise's framing (12 rows) makes coalesce sufficient.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Picks repartition over coalesce; pays for a shuffle when no shuffle is needed.

Option C: Picks single-file output via repartition; restrictive for downstream parallelism and adds shuffle cost.

Option D: Picks single-file output via coalesce; restrictive for downstream parallelism (and as Q3 shows, comes with a serious cost on the upstream side).

fields.label: Why is coalesce(1) NOT the right edit, even though it produces a single file with no shuffle?
options: coalesce(1) is incorrect because Spark's coalesce operator falls back to a shuffle when the target partition count is below 2, and the implicit shuffle defeats the no-shuffle property that motivates choosing coalesce over repartition for this kind of edit.

coalesce(1) is incorrect because it produces a single file but the file's row group structure becomes degenerate at 12 rows, with the single-row-group file losing the per-row-group statistics that Parquet uses for predicate pushdown on subsequent reads.

coalesce(1) is incorrect because it forces the entire upstream computation onto a single executor task; the aggregation that produces the 12-row output runs serially on one core, eliminating the parallelism the pipeline was using to process the 1.2M Silver rows.

coalesce(1) is incorrect because the output partition count of 1 conflicts with the broadcast-eligible threshold; the writer treats the single partition as a broadcast candidate and copies it to every executor before writing, producing a single file but at a higher cost than necessary.
fields.correctAnswer: coalesce(1) is incorrect because it forces the entire upstream computation onto a single executor task; the aggregation that produces the 12-row output runs serially on one core, eliminating the parallelism the pipeline was using to process the 1.2M Silver rows.
fields.rationale:
coalesce(N) does not introduce a shuffle, but it also does not isolate its effect to the write step alone. Coalescing to a single partition propagates upward: every step before the coalesce that runs in parallel must funnel into a single task before the coalesce point. For coalesce(1), this means the aggregation that processes 1.2M rows runs on one core. The other options invent specific failure modes (forced shuffle below 2, degenerate row groups, broadcast eligibility) that are not how coalesce works.

When this answer is wrong: If the upstream computation were trivially small (e.g., reading 100 rows and writing them out), coalesce(1) would be fine because there is no parallel work to lose. The exercise's framing (1.2M Silver rows processed upstream) makes the parallelism loss the binding cost.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Invents a 'shuffle below 2' rule that does not exist.

Option B: Reaches for row-group statistics as the issue; statistics work fine on small files.

Option D: Invents a broadcast-via-coalesce mechanism that is not real.

fields.label: If the engineer had chosen repartition(1) instead of coalesce(12), what would happen?
options: The pipeline would produce a single file via an explicit shuffle to one partition; the upstream aggregation runs in parallel as before, the shuffle redistributes the 12 output rows to a single task, and the single task writes the file. Slightly slower than coalesce(12) but correct.

The pipeline would produce a single file but the shuffle to one partition would error out because Spark refuses to shuffle to a partition count below the cluster's minimum task count; the engineer would have to use coalesce(1) instead to achieve the single-file output.

The pipeline would produce one file but the shuffle to a single partition forces all 1.2M Silver rows through one executor task at the shuffle step, defeating the parallelism the pipeline was using to process the Silver layer before the aggregation.

The pipeline would produce one file but the explicit shuffle invalidates Catalyst's broadcast-join optimization for the upstream substations join, and the join falls back to sort-merge as a result of the repartition step inserted between the join and the write.
fields.correctAnswer: The pipeline would produce a single file via an explicit shuffle to one partition; the upstream aggregation runs in parallel as before, the shuffle redistributes the 12 output rows to a single task, and the single task writes the file. Slightly slower than coalesce(12) but correct.
fields.rationale:
repartition introduces an explicit shuffle, which acts as a barrier between upstream parallelism and the new partition count. The aggregation runs on the original partition count in parallel, the shuffle redistributes the 12 output rows to a single task, and only the final write step is single-threaded. Slightly slower than coalesce(12) because of the shuffle, but the upstream parallelism is preserved. The other options invent error conditions, parallelism collapse, or join-strategy regressions that do not actually occur with repartition.

When this answer is wrong: If the upstream computation produces enormous data (e.g., 100 GB) before the aggregation, the shuffle to a single partition would funnel all that data through one task and become a bottleneck. The exercise's framing (12-row aggregate output) makes the shuffle to one partition cheap.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Invents a Spark constraint on minimum partition count that does not exist.

Option C: Conflates repartition (which is a barrier) with coalesce (which is not); repartition preserves upstream parallelism.

Option D: Invents a join-strategy regression triggered by repartition; does not happen.

fields.label: After the fix, the engineer notices that the writer takes 4 seconds longer than before. Why?
options: The 4-second delay reflects the extra Parquet footer writes that the new layout produces; with 12 files instead of 200, the writer writes 12 footers but each footer is larger and the per-footer write cost is higher than the previous configuration averaged across files.

The 4-second delay reflects the post-aggregate merge step that coalesce introduces; merging 200 partitions into 12 takes a small constant time (proportional to the partition count and not to the data volume) which the previous unmerged write did not pay.

The 4-second delay reflects the shuffle that coalesce introduces when the target partition count is significantly lower than the current one; the implicit shuffle moves data across executors before writing, which the previous configuration did not need.

The 4-second delay reflects the write-side compression overhead that larger files incur; with each Parquet file holding more rows, the columnar compression has more data to compress per file and the per-file compression CPU dominates the write time.
fields.correctAnswer: The 4-second delay reflects the post-aggregate merge step that coalesce introduces; merging 200 partitions into 12 takes a small constant time (proportional to the partition count and not to the data volume) which the previous unmerged write did not pay.
fields.rationale:
The merge step that the operator performs to reduce partition count carries a small fixed coordination overhead, scaling with how many partitions must be combined rather than with how much data flows through. Going from 200 partitions to 12 produces about 4 seconds of overhead from coordinating the merge across executors, which is independent of how few rows are involved. Footer writes (option A) are smaller than this. coalesce does not introduce a shuffle (option C). Compression overhead (option D) is negligible at 12 rows.

When this answer is wrong: If the row count were much larger and coalesce had to physically move significant data, the cost would be dominated by data movement rather than coordination. The exercise's framing (small data volume, partition-count change) keeps coordination as the dominant cost.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Picks footer overhead; smaller than coordination cost.

Option C: Asserts coalesce introduces a shuffle; it does not (this is the defining property of coalesce vs repartition).

Option D: Picks compression overhead; negligible at 12 rows.
