tasks.title: The 49MB Reference Table

description.context: A NordGrid pipeline joins the daily 3.2 TB readings table to a substations reference table. The team's lead notices the join takes 22 minutes when she expected 2-3 minutes for what looks like a broadcast-eligible reference join. The substations table has 18,000 rows and is 49 MB on disk in Parquet. The cluster has spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold set to its default of 10 MB. The lead asks the engineer to read the join setup and predict which physical strategy will fire under each of four configurations.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid pipeline joins the daily 3.2 TB readings table to a substations reference table. The team's lead notices the join takes 22 minutes when she expected 2-3 minutes for what looks like a broadcast-eligible reference join. The substations table has 18,000 rows and is 49 MB on disk in Parquet. The cluster has spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold set to its default of 10 MB. The lead asks the engineer to read the join setup and predict which physical strategy will fire under each of four configurations.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: The pipeline runs nightly with a 90-minute SLA. At 22 minutes the join is the dominant stage and the team has been told that getting the join to broadcast would cut the pipeline runtime by roughly an order of magnitude. The decision is which configuration change to ship.

evidence.title: Platform context
evidence.content: The Customer team OWNS this pipeline. Three other pipelines on the cluster also join against substations. The team is debating whether to fix the configuration globally (all four pipelines benefit) or only for this pipeline (others might have reasons for the current strategy). The Substations team OWNS the substations table and has just confirmed that 49 MB is the steady-state size — it has been growing at about 2 MB per year as new substations are added across the 12-region NordGrid expansion.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (Bronze readings, 3.2 TB), substations.csv (18,000 rows, 49 MB Parquet)

evidence.label: Tables
Query
evidence.content:
result = (
    spark.table('nordgrid.readings')
        .filter(col('date') == today)
        .join(spark.table('nordgrid.substations'), 'substation_id', 'left')
        .select('meter_id', 'daily_kw', 'substation_name', 'capacity_mw')
)

evidence.label: Candidate Configurations
evidence.content:
[
  "Default (autoBroadcastJoinThreshold = 10 MB), no hints",
  "Default threshold, add broadcast(substations) hint to the query",
  "Raise autoBroadcastJoinThreshold to 50 MB cluster-wide, no hints",
  "Default threshold, enable AQE (which can convert at runtime)"
]

fields.label: Under the default configuration with no hints, which join strategy will the planner choose?
options: SortMergeJoin will fire because substations at 49 MB exceeds the 10 MB broadcast threshold; both sides are shuffled on substation_id, sorted, and merged. The 3.2 TB shuffle on the readings side is what drives the 22-minute runtime to its current value.

BroadcastHashJoin will fire because substations is small relative to readings; the planner picks broadcast based on the relative size ratio between the two tables rather than against the absolute threshold setting on the cluster.

ShuffledHashJoin will fire because substations is too large to broadcast but too small to merit a sort-merge; the planner picks the middle strategy that hashes the smaller side after a single shuffle on the join key.

SortMergeJoin will fire on the date predicate's pushdown side and BroadcastHashJoin on the post-filter side; the planner splits the join across two phases when one side has a partition filter and the other does not in this kind of mixed workload.
fields.correctAnswer: SortMergeJoin will fire because substations at 49 MB exceeds the 10 MB broadcast threshold; both sides are shuffled on substation_id, sorted, and merged. The 3.2 TB shuffle on the readings side is what drives the 22-minute runtime to its current value.
fields.rationale:
The substations table at 49 MB sits above the configured broadcast threshold of 10 MB, so the planner does not pick broadcast. The default fallback is SortMergeJoin, which shuffles both sides on substation_id. The 3.2 TB shuffle on the readings side is what dominates the 22-minute runtime. Other options invent strategies (relative-size broadcast, ShuffledHashJoin as a middle ground, split-strategy execution) that the planner does not actually use here.

When this answer is wrong: If autoBroadcastJoinThreshold had been raised earlier (or the cost-based optimiser was configured differently), the broadcast could fire even with 49 MB. The exercise's framing (default 10 MB threshold) makes SortMergeJoin the planner's choice.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Invents relative-size broadcast logic; the planner uses the absolute threshold.

Option C: Picks ShuffledHashJoin as a middle ground; Spark's planner does not use SHJ as a default for this size range.

Option D: Invents split-strategy execution; the join runs as a single physical operator.

fields.label: Under configuration 2 (default threshold + broadcast hint), what fires?
options: BroadcastHashJoin fires because the hint overrides the threshold check; Spark broadcasts substations regardless of size, the 49 MB transfers to every executor once, and the readings side stays in place. Runtime drops because the 3.2 TB shuffle disappears.

BroadcastHashJoin fires only on executors with enough memory to hold the 49 MB broadcast; executors below the memory threshold fall back to SortMergeJoin for their portion of the workload, producing a mixed-strategy execution across the cluster.

BroadcastHashJoin fires because the hint requests it, but the broadcast itself triggers a check against driver memory; if the driver has spare memory the broadcast proceeds, otherwise the hint is treated as advisory and the planner reverts to SortMergeJoin for safety.

BroadcastHashJoin fires but the hint is paired with an implicit cap on broadcast size at twice the configured threshold; for 49 MB at a 10 MB default threshold, the cap is 20 MB and the hint is rejected with a planning-time warning that falls back to SortMergeJoin.
fields.correctAnswer: BroadcastHashJoin fires because the hint requests it, but the broadcast itself triggers a check against driver memory; if the driver has spare memory the broadcast proceeds, otherwise the hint is treated as advisory and the planner reverts to SortMergeJoin for safety.
fields.rationale:
BroadcastHashJoin is what the optimizer chooses, but the actual broadcast operation runs through the driver — it collects the broadcast side and ships it to executors. If the driver has insufficient memory, the planner falls back to SortMergeJoin to avoid driver OOM. With 49 MB and a typical driver memory configuration the broadcast succeeds, but the safety check is real. Option A omits the driver-memory check; option B invents per-executor fallback; option D invents an implicit cap.

When this answer is wrong: If the driver memory were aggressively constrained (a small driver in a serverless cluster), the hint could fail and option D's fallback behavior would describe the actual outcome. The exercise's framing (typical driver) makes the hint succeed.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Omits the driver-memory safety check; broadcast goes through the driver.

Option B: Invents per-executor strategy mixing; Spark uses one strategy per join operator.

Option D: Invents an implicit cap at 2x the threshold; no such rule exists.

fields.label: Under configuration 3 (autoBroadcastJoinThreshold raised to 50 MB), what fires for this query? What's the side effect on other pipelines?
options: BroadcastHashJoin fires for this query because 49 MB now falls under 50 MB; other pipelines are unaffected because the threshold change is scoped to the current SparkSession and the configuration applies only at the session level when set globally.

BroadcastHashJoin fires for this query because substations now qualifies for broadcast; the same threshold change affects every pipeline on the cluster, which can be a benefit (other pipelines also broadcast their reference tables) or a risk (a previously-large table now broadcasts when it should not).

BroadcastHashJoin fires for this query but only when AQE is also enabled across the SparkSession; the 50 MB threshold by itself is treated as advisory and requires AQE's runtime confirmation step to actually broadcast tables that sit above the original 10 MB default value.

BroadcastHashJoin fires for this query because the cluster-wide threshold change applies to every join planner pass; the side effect is that any reference table between 10 MB and 50 MB across the cluster's four pipelines now broadcasts, with the corresponding broadcast-memory cost on every executor.
fields.correctAnswer: BroadcastHashJoin fires for this query because the cluster-wide threshold change applies to every join planner pass; the side effect is that any reference table between 10 MB and 50 MB across the cluster's four pipelines now broadcasts, with the corresponding broadcast-memory cost on every executor.
fields.rationale:
spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold is a cluster-wide setting (when set in spark-defaults.conf). Raising it to 50 MB makes substations broadcast for this pipeline and for any other pipeline whose join planning pass evaluates a similar reference table. The side effect is real: any table between 10 MB and 50 MB across the cluster now broadcasts. Other options either incorrectly scope the change (A claims session-only when set globally, B is correct in spirit but D is more precise about which tables fire), or invent AQE confirmation requirements (C).

When this answer is wrong: If the threshold were set in the team's job config rather than the cluster config (e.g., in spark.conf.set at the start of the job), it would be session-scoped and option A's framing would be accurate. The exercise's framing (cluster-wide raise) makes the side effect real.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Asserts session-scope for a cluster-wide configuration; incorrect when the change is in spark-defaults.conf.

Option B: Names the right outcome but less precisely than D; both broadcast and the side effect are correctly named in D.

Option C: Invents AQE confirmation requirement; the threshold operates at planning time, AQE is independent.

fields.label: With AQE enabled but no other configuration changes, what does AQE do at runtime?
options: AQE converts the SortMergeJoin to a BroadcastHashJoin during the initial query compilation by inspecting the catalog statistics for both tables; the conversion happens before any stage runs and the resulting plan does not include a SortMergeJoin step at all.

AQE inspects the post-shuffle data sizes after the first stage and converts the join to broadcast IF the actual data after the shuffle is smaller than the threshold; for substations at 49 MB the post-shuffle size is still 49 MB and the conversion does not fire under the default 10 MB threshold.

AQE detects skew in the substations data and applies a skew-handling broadcast on the affected keys; the substation_id distribution determines which keys broadcast and which remain in the original join strategy through the post-stage conversion.

AQE replans the join based on the larger side's actual size after the date filter applies; once the readings side narrows to one day's data (~3.2 TB / 365 ≈ 9 GB), the planner reconsiders the strategy and may broadcast the smaller original substations side.
fields.correctAnswer: AQE inspects the post-shuffle data sizes after the first stage and converts the join to broadcast IF the actual data after the shuffle is smaller than the threshold; for substations at 49 MB the post-shuffle size is still 49 MB and the conversion does not fire under the default 10 MB threshold.
fields.rationale:
AQE's broadcast-conversion rule fires when post-shuffle data size on a side falls under the broadcast threshold. The substations side does not shrink during execution — there is no filter, just the 49 MB reference table. After the shuffle the side is still 49 MB, exceeding the 10 MB default threshold, so AQE does not convert. The other options either invent compile-time conversion (A), invoke skew handling (C), or describe a different reasoning path (D, which works on the readings side rather than the substations side).

When this answer is wrong: If a filter on substations were added (e.g., filter to active substations only), the post-shuffle size could drop below the threshold and AQE would convert. The exercise's framing (no filter on substations) keeps the post-shuffle size at 49 MB.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Conflates AQE with cost-based optimization at compile time; AQE is runtime.

Option C: Invokes skew handling as the conversion mechanism; skew handling is a different AQE feature.

Option D: Reasons about the readings side; the broadcast-conversion check applies to the smaller side.

fields.label: The team is choosing between configuration 2 (hint) and configuration 3 (raise threshold). Which is the better choice?
options: Configuration 2 (hint) is better because it scopes the broadcast decision to this specific query; the other three pipelines on the cluster keep their current behavior, and the team that owns each pipeline gets to decide whether to broadcast their respective reference tables.

Configuration 3 (raise threshold) is better because it applies once globally and benefits every pipeline; the operational simplicity outweighs the small per-team-decision concern, and any pipeline that does not want to broadcast can override with a no-broadcast hint at the call site.

Configuration 2 (hint) is better because it does not require a cluster-wide configuration change; the team can ship the change without coordinating with the other pipeline owners, and the hint is reversible if the broadcast turns out to be problematic on inspection.

Configuration 3 (raise threshold) is better because the substations table is shared across pipelines; if four pipelines all join to substations, four broadcasts of 49 MB are nearly indistinguishable from one broadcast at 49 MB and the threshold raise gives consistent strategy across all consumers.
fields.correctAnswer: Configuration 2 (hint) is better because it scopes the broadcast decision to this specific query; the other three pipelines on the cluster keep their current behavior, and the team that owns each pipeline gets to decide whether to broadcast their respective reference tables.
fields.rationale:
Hints are local; threshold changes are global. The hint approach lets each team make its own broadcast decision based on its own pipeline's data. The threshold change forces consistency, which is good when the team has visibility into all four pipelines but problematic when they do not. The other pipelines' owners may have reasons (driver memory, broadcast contention, table volatility) that the configuration change would override silently.

When this answer is wrong: If all four pipelines were owned by the same team and shared similar workload characteristics, the threshold raise would be cleaner and option B's argument would dominate. The exercise's framing (cross-team pipelines) makes the local-decision argument the strongest.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Argues operational simplicity over per-team autonomy; correct on platforms with single ownership.

Option C: Names the right answer (hint) but for a weaker reason (avoiding coordination); the per-team-decision argument is stronger.

Option D: Argues consistency without considering that the four teams have legitimate reasons to differ.

fields.label: If the substations table grows to 200 MB next year (well above any reasonable broadcast threshold), what should happen?
options: The hint configuration would silently broadcast a 200 MB table to every executor, producing memory pressure that surfaces as task failures or executor OOM events; the team would need to revisit whether the broadcast is still appropriate at the new size on each Spark upgrade.

Spark's planner would automatically refuse to broadcast 200 MB even with the hint, falling back to SortMergeJoin; the hint is documented as a request rather than a directive, and the planner reserves the right to override for safety on tables above a hard cap.

AQE would intercept the broadcast attempt and convert it to ShuffledHashJoin; the runtime size check on the broadcast side reroutes large tables to a hashed shuffle strategy that approximates broadcast performance without the per-executor memory cost.

The team would have to remove the hint (or lower the cluster threshold) and accept SortMergeJoin; broadcasting 200 MB to every executor scales with executor count and is genuinely expensive at any reasonable cluster size, so the broadcast strategy stops being the right one above some size.
fields.correctAnswer: The team would have to remove the hint (or lower the cluster threshold) and accept SortMergeJoin; broadcasting 200 MB to every executor scales with executor count and is genuinely expensive at any reasonable cluster size, so the broadcast strategy stops being the right one above some size.
fields.rationale:
A 200 MB broadcast scales poorly across the cluster: shipping it to 100 executors moves 20 GB across the network per query, and each executor holds the whole table in memory. At some size the cost outweighs the SortMergeJoin shuffle cost. The team has to revisit the strategy when the size crosses that line. Other options either describe ongoing pain (A's task failures), invent automatic refusals (B's hard cap), or invent AQE conversions to ShuffledHashJoin (C, which AQE does not do automatically for this case).

When this answer is wrong: If the cluster has a small executor count (e.g., 8 executors) and very large per-executor memory (256 GB), broadcasting 200 MB might still be cheaper than a sort-merge shuffle and the team could keep the hint. The exercise's framing (large cluster, typical sizing) makes the broadcast cost prohibitive.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Describes the symptom (OOM) rather than the proactive remediation.

Option B: Invents a planner safety override; the planner respects hints unless driver memory is the constraint.

Option C: Invents an automatic AQE conversion to ShuffledHashJoin; not how AQE responds to oversized broadcasts.

tasks.title: The Join That Got Faster When the Filter Got Tighter

description.context: A NordGrid analytics engineer modifies a query: the filter on customer_type goes from 'IN (RESIDENTIAL, COMMERCIAL, INDUSTRIAL, AGRICULTURAL)' to 'IN (INDUSTRIAL)'. The query joins meters to a tariff_history table (45 MB on disk). The new tighter filter is expected to make the query slower (more selective filter, fewer rows match — but also less work overall, so it should at worst be the same speed). Instead the runtime drops from 18 minutes to 90 seconds. The lead asks the engineer to read the Spark UI for both runs and explain the speedup.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid analytics engineer modifies a query: the filter on customer_type goes from 'IN (RESIDENTIAL, COMMERCIAL, INDUSTRIAL, AGRICULTURAL)' to 'IN (INDUSTRIAL)'. The query joins meters to a tariff_history table (45 MB on disk). The new tighter filter is expected to make the query slower (more selective filter, fewer rows match — but also less work overall, so it should at worst be the same speed). Instead the runtime drops from 18 minutes to 90 seconds. The lead asks the engineer to read the Spark UI for both runs and explain the speedup.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: AQE is enabled cluster-wide. The team is considering whether to depend on this AQE-driven speedup for other queries that join against tariff_history. The decision depends on understanding what AQE actually did and when the same pattern would or would not fire elsewhere.

evidence.title: Platform context
evidence.content: The Customer team OWNS the meters table; the Billing team OWNS tariff_history (45 MB; the 'history' part is what makes it bigger than the simple tariffs table). The Analytics team is the consumer running this query. AQE was enabled three months ago by the Platform team as part of a Spark 3.4 upgrade.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (Bronze, 1.2M rows for one day; customer_type IN one of four values), tariff_history.csv (45 MB; one row per (customer_type, region, valid_from); ~ 8 MB per customer_type post-filter)

evidence.title: Query Before
evidence.content:
(meters
    .filter(col('customer_type').isin('RESIDENTIAL', 'COMMERCIAL', 'INDUSTRIAL', 'AGRICULTURAL'))
    .join(tariff_history, ['customer_type', 'region'], 'left'))

evidence.label: Query After
evidence.content:
(meters
    .filter(col('customer_type') == 'INDUSTRIAL')
    .join(tariff_history, ['customer_type', 'region'], 'left'))

evidence.label: Spark Ui Before
evidence.content:
Stages: 4 (Scan, Exchange-meters, Exchange-tariff_history, SortMergeJoin)
Join operator: SortMergeJoin
Shuffle write (meters side): 320 MB
Shuffle write (tariff_history side): 45 MB
Total stage time: 18 min
No AQE conversion fired (post-shuffle data on tariff_history side: 45 MB, exceeds 10 MB threshold)

evidence.label: Spark Ui After
evidence.content:
Stages: 3 (Scan, Exchange-meters, BroadcastHashJoin) [AQE Plan Update event logged]
Join operator: SortMergeJoin -> BroadcastHashJoin (AQE conversion at stage 2 boundary)
Shuffle write (meters side): 80 MB
Shuffle write (tariff_history side): collected as broadcast (post-conversion)
Total stage time: 90 sec
AQE conversion fired: post-shuffle data on tariff_history side after filter pushdown: 8 MB

fields.label: What did AQE do during the second query that it did not do during the first?
options: AQE detected skew in the customer_type distribution and applied skew-handling to balance the join's task load; the tighter filter reduced the keys that participated in the skew handling, which produced the runtime speedup observed in the Spark UI metrics.

AQE converted the SortMergeJoin to a BroadcastHashJoin at the boundary between stages, after observing that the tariff_history side after filter pushdown was 8 MB — below the 10 MB broadcast threshold; the conversion eliminated the meters-side shuffle entirely.

AQE coalesced the post-shuffle partitions on the meters side from 200 down to a smaller number that matched the post-filter row count; the smaller partition count let the cluster process the meters side in fewer waves than the original configuration.

AQE rewrote the join's physical operator to a streaming join because the tariff_history table was small enough to fit in memory; the streaming join skipped the traditional shuffle steps and processed records directly from the meters side as they arrived from the scan.
fields.correctAnswer: AQE converted the SortMergeJoin to a BroadcastHashJoin at the boundary between stages, after observing that the tariff_history side after filter pushdown was 8 MB — below the 10 MB broadcast threshold; the conversion eliminated the meters-side shuffle entirely.
fields.rationale:
The Spark UI for the second run logs an AQE Plan Update event and shows SortMergeJoin -> BroadcastHashJoin. The conversion happened at the stage boundary after the post-shuffle size on the tariff_history side came in at 8 MB (45 MB filtered down by customer_type). 8 MB is below the 10 MB threshold, so AQE converted. The other options invent skew handling, partition coalescing, or streaming joins that the Spark UI does not show.

When this answer is wrong: If the post-shuffle size had been 12 MB (just above threshold), AQE would not have converted and the speedup would not have happened. The exercise's framing (8 MB post-filter) makes the conversion fire.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names skew handling, a different AQE feature; the SQL UI does not show skew evidence.

Option C: Names partition coalescing; the SQL UI shows the join strategy changed, not just the partition count.

Option D: Invents a streaming-join conversion that AQE does not do.

fields.label: Why did the same conversion NOT fire in the first query?
options: The tariff_history side post-shuffle was 45 MB in the first query, which is above the 10 MB broadcast threshold; AQE's broadcast-conversion check evaluates the actual post-shuffle size against the threshold and the 45 MB exceeded the limit at every check point during the run.

AQE's broadcast conversion runs only when the join key cardinality is below a threshold; the first query had four customer_type values, which exceeded the cardinality threshold AQE uses to decide whether to attempt a broadcast conversion at the stage boundary.

The first query had four parallel branches in the plan because the IN filter expanded into four separate predicates; AQE's broadcast conversion is disabled when the plan has multiple parallel branches that share the same join target table.

AQE's broadcast conversion requires statistics on both sides of the join to be fresh; the tariff_history table's statistics were stale at the time of the first run, and the conversion was skipped pending the next ANALYZE schedule for the Billing team's reference data.
fields.correctAnswer: The tariff_history side post-shuffle was 45 MB in the first query, which is above the 10 MB broadcast threshold; AQE's broadcast-conversion check evaluates the actual post-shuffle size against the threshold and the 45 MB exceeded the limit at every check point during the run.
fields.rationale:
All four customer types contribute their rows when the wider IN-list filter is in place, leaving the tariff_history reference at its full 45 MB. AQE evaluates post-shuffle size against the threshold, and 45 MB exceeds 10 MB, so the conversion does not fire. Other options invent specific gating mechanisms (cardinality limits, parallel-branch detection, statistics freshness) that are not how AQE's broadcast-conversion check works.

When this answer is wrong: If a different AQE setting (e.g., adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold) had been raised above 45 MB, the first query's broadcast conversion would also have fired. The exercise's framing (default 10 MB AQE threshold) makes 45 MB exceed it.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Invents a join-key-cardinality threshold that AQE does not have.

Option C: Invents a parallel-branch detection that AQE does not have.

Option D: Asserts AQE requires fresh statistics; AQE works at runtime regardless of compile-time statistics.

fields.label: The team wants to make the broadcast conversion fire reliably for all queries against tariff_history. Which approach gives the most reliable result?
options: Add a broadcast hint to every query against tariff_history; the hint guarantees the broadcast strategy regardless of post-shuffle size and avoids the dependency on AQE's runtime decision making process across the cluster's varying workload.

Raise the AQE broadcast threshold (spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold) so 45 MB falls under it; AQE's broadcast conversion will then fire on the unfiltered case as well as the filtered case, giving consistent broadcast behavior across all customer_type filters.

Pre-filter or pre-aggregate the tariff_history table into a smaller per-customer_type slice that consumers join against; the smaller table guarantees broadcast eligibility at any threshold and decouples the strategy from AQE's runtime decisions.

Enable AQE skew handling with a low skew threshold; the skew-handling layer redistributes the join's work in a way that approximates broadcast behavior even when the table itself is too large to broadcast under the standard threshold setting.
fields.correctAnswer: Pre-filter or pre-aggregate the tariff_history table into a smaller per-customer_type slice that consumers join against; the smaller table guarantees broadcast eligibility at any threshold and decouples the strategy from AQE's runtime decisions.
fields.rationale:
The most reliable path is to ensure the joined-against table is genuinely small at the catalog level: produce smaller filtered or aggregated copies and have consumers join those. This makes the strategy reliable across all consumers without depending on runtime decisions. Hints (option A) work but require touching every query and ignore the underlying issue (the table is too big for unconditional broadcast). Raising the AQE threshold (option B) trades safety for reliability — broadcasting 45 MB to every executor is wasteful. Skew handling (option D) is a different mechanism that does not approximate broadcast.

When this answer is wrong: If pre-aggregation is operationally complex (e.g., the tariff_history table is owned by a different team that cannot ship per-consumer slices), option A's hints become the practical answer. The exercise's framing (single team owns the slice transform) makes pre-filtering feasible.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Picks per-query hints; works but does not address the underlying size.

Option B: Raises the threshold past 45 MB; broadcasts a large table unconditionally.

Option D: Reaches for skew handling as broadcast substitute; different mechanism.

fields.label: If AQE were disabled (or not yet upgraded to a version that supports broadcast conversion), what would the engineer have to do to get the same speedup?
options: The engineer would have to broadcast the tariff_history table eagerly using broadcast() at the call site; the eager broadcast bypasses the threshold check and forces broadcast even at 45 MB, achieving the same speedup as the AQE conversion provided in the second query run.

The engineer would have to pre-filter tariff_history to the relevant customer_type before the join; the pre-filter shrinks tariff_history below the broadcast threshold at compile time so the planner picks broadcast without needing AQE's runtime conversion to fire.

The engineer would have to switch to a ShuffledHashJoin via a hint; without AQE the planner cannot pick the optimal strategy automatically, and the explicit ShuffledHashJoin gives most of the broadcast performance without the per-executor memory cost of true broadcast.

The engineer would have to materialise the filtered tariff_history into a temporary table, run ANALYZE on it to record the post-filter size in the catalog, then join the meters side against the materialised version; the materialisation is what makes the small size visible to the planner without runtime support.
fields.correctAnswer: The engineer would have to materialise the filtered tariff_history into a temporary table, run ANALYZE on it to record the post-filter size in the catalog, then join the meters side against the materialised version; the materialisation is what makes the small size visible to the planner without runtime support.
fields.rationale:
Without runtime conversion, the only way to get the planner to pick broadcast is to make the catalog-recorded size genuinely small — which means writing out a smaller materialised version with fresh statistics. Eager broadcast() (option A) works at small scales but ignores the threshold check that exists for a reason. Pre-filter on the unmaterialised version (option B) does not change the catalog-recorded size. ShuffledHashJoin via hint (option C) is a different strategy that does not give broadcast performance.

When this answer is wrong: If broadcast() at 45 MB is operationally safe on this cluster (sufficient driver memory, executor memory), option A is the simpler change. The exercise's framing (asking what the engineer 'would have to' do) implies the conservative approach with explicit materialisation.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Uses eager broadcast at sizes the threshold would refuse; works but bypasses the safety check.

Option B: Pre-filters the unmaterialised version; the planner still sees catalog-recorded size.

Option C: Picks ShuffledHashJoin; different physical strategy that does not produce broadcast performance.

fields.label: Looking at the Spark UI more closely, the engineer notices the meters side shuffle dropped from 320 MB to 80 MB in the second run. Why?
options: The narrower customer_type filter reduced the meters-side row count by 75%, so the post-filter shuffle volume scaled proportionally; this is independent of the join strategy and reflects the work the filter does upstream of the join's shuffle in the SQL UI metrics.

The AQE broadcast conversion eliminates the meters-side shuffle entirely; the 80 MB the SQL UI reports is the meters-side output after the broadcast join completes (a side-output of the BroadcastHashJoin's local materialisation step), not a true shuffle in the original sense.

The narrower filter's selectivity propagated to the meters-side shuffle write through Catalyst's predicate pushdown; the smaller volume of rows that actually reach the join is what the meters-side shuffle wrote, with the per-row size of each row unchanged from the previous run.

The AQE coalesce-shuffle-partitions feature reduced the partition count on the meters side after observing the smaller post-filter data; fewer partitions means smaller per-partition shuffle write totals reported in the SQL UI for the meters side after AQE applied.
fields.correctAnswer: The AQE broadcast conversion eliminates the meters-side shuffle entirely; the 80 MB the SQL UI reports is the meters-side output after the broadcast join completes (a side-output of the BroadcastHashJoin's local materialisation step), not a true shuffle in the original sense.
fields.rationale:
When AQE converts the join to broadcast, the meters-side shuffle is no longer needed — broadcast joins do not shuffle the larger side. The 80 MB the SQL UI shows is the meters-side data after the (now-redundant) shuffle stage that AQE could not undo retroactively (the stage had already started). Option A's filter selectivity is part of the story but doesn't explain why the SQL UI still shows a shuffle write at all. Option C's predicate pushdown is real but doesn't reduce the meters-side shuffle by 75% in this scenario. Option D's coalesce-shuffle-partitions reduces partition count, not shuffle volume.

When this answer is wrong: If AQE had not converted the join (a different scenario where post-shuffle size exceeded the threshold), the meters-side shuffle would have proceeded normally and option A's filter-selectivity explanation would describe the dominant effect. The exercise's framing (AQE conversion fired) makes the broadcast-side-effect the primary cause.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names filter selectivity as the dominant cause; the broadcast conversion is the more direct cause of the shuffle volume drop.

Option C: Conflates predicate pushdown (compile time) with runtime AQE effects (runtime).

Option D: Confuses partition count reduction with shuffle volume reduction.

description.context: A NordGrid pipeline that groups meter readings by region runs in 42 minutes when the team expected 6-8 minutes. The Spark UI for the shuffle stage shows 195 tasks finishing in 18 to 35 seconds and 5 tasks taking 38 to 42 minutes each. Total stage time is 42 minutes (governed by the longest task). The team's lead pulls up the task duration histogram and the per-task shuffle read bytes and asks the engineer to identify which mitigation matches the signature shown.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.content: A NordGrid pipeline that groups meter readings by region runs in 42 minutes when the team expected 6-8 minutes. The team's lead pulls up the task duration histogram and the per-task shuffle read bytes and asks the engineer to identify which mitigation matches the signature shown.

evidence.label: Candidate Mitigations
evidence.content:
[
  "Enable AQE skew handling (spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true) — splits large partitions at runtime",
  "Salt the join key by appending a random suffix to region values, then aggregate twice",
  "Isolate the skewed regions into a separate pipeline run with a different partition count",
  "Increase spark.sql.shuffle.partitions from 200 to 600 to spread the load more finely across tasks"

fields.label: Which signature does the task histogram show?
options: Memory pressure across most executors with a few executors holding more data than the rest; the metric pattern reflects uneven memory consumption per executor and the stage runtime is governed by the executors carrying the heavier load through the shuffle stage of the pipeline.

Slow tasks distributed across the cluster with no specific partition pattern; the runtime gap between p50 and the max task reflects general cluster variance from co-tenant workloads competing for cluster resources during the stage's execution window.

Partition skew on the join key, where a small number of partitions hold disproportionately more data than the rest; the per-task shuffle read bytes confirm the imbalance (1.5 MB median vs. 120 MB max), and the wall-clock is governed by the longest task.

Spill to disk on a subset of partitions whose data exceeds executor memory; the long-running tasks are the ones that spill, and the runtime is the disk-write cost the spilling partitions pay during the shuffle write phase of the stage.
fields.correctAnswer: Partition skew on the join key, where a small number of partitions hold disproportionately more data than the rest; the per-task shuffle read bytes confirm the imbalance (1.5 MB median vs. 120 MB max), and the wall-clock is governed by the longest task.
fields.rationale:
The signature is classic data skew: median shuffle-read at 1.5 MB and max at 120 MB (an 80x ratio) with five tasks dominating wall-clock. The per-task shuffle read bytes show the imbalance directly. Option A is memory pressure (different signature: GC time spikes, executor restarts). Option B is general cluster variance (different signature: scattered slow tasks across many partitions). Option D is spill (different signature: disk write counter spikes, not shuffle read imbalance).

When this answer is wrong: If the per-task shuffle read bytes had been uniform but the duration histogram still showed the same shape, the cause would be per-task work imbalance rather than data imbalance and option A or B's diagnosis could apply. The exercise's framing (shuffle bytes show the imbalance directly) makes skew the structural answer.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names memory pressure as the cause; different signature (GC time spikes).

Option B: Treats the slow tasks as general variance; the per-partition pattern contradicts this.

Option D: Names spill; spill shows up as disk write spikes, not shuffle read imbalance.

fields.label: Which mitigation matches the skew signature most directly for a groupBy (not a join)?
options: AQE skew handling (spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled) splits large partitions at runtime; the conversion fires on detected skew above a configured ratio and runtime, redistributing the heavy partitions across additional tasks for the remaining shuffle to process.

Salting the key by appending a random suffix is the classic skew-mitigation for groupBy aggregations; the random suffix distributes one heavy key across multiple partitions during the first aggregation, with a second aggregation that re-collapses the suffix back into a single per-key result.

Isolating the skewed regions into a separate pipeline run gives each load profile its own partition count and resource pool; the heavy regions process under one configuration and the light regions under another, with the union producing the final output across both.

Raising spark.sql.shuffle.partitions from 200 to 600 spreads keys more finely across tasks; with three times as many partitions, the heavy keys split across more tasks and the per-task load drops proportionally to the partition-count increase.
fields.correctAnswer: Salting the key by appending a random suffix is the classic skew-mitigation for groupBy aggregations; the random suffix distributes one heavy key across multiple partitions during the first aggregation, with a second aggregation that re-collapses the suffix back into a single per-key result.
fields.rationale:
Salting is the classic fix for groupBy skew. A random suffix is appended to each row's key, splitting one heavy key across multiple post-aggregate partitions during a first aggregation pass. A second aggregation removes the suffix and collapses back to the original key. The cost is one extra shuffle. AQE skew handling (option A) applies to joins, not groupBy. Pipeline isolation (option C) and partition-count raises (option D) do not address skew structurally.

When this answer is wrong: If the operation were a join (not a groupBy), AQE skew handling (option A) would be the direct match because AQE's skew layer is join-specific. The exercise's framing (groupBy aggregation) makes salting the right fit.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Picks AQE skew handling without noting it is join-specific.

Option C: Picks pipeline isolation as a partition-level fix; treats symptom not cause.

Option D: Picks partition count raise; covered in next question as a non-fix for skew.

fields.label: Why does raising shuffle partitions from 200 to 600 NOT fix this kind of skew?
options: Raising partition count helps when the data is uniformly distributed across keys but the per-task data is too large; with skew, the heavy keys land on whichever partitions they hash to, and the extra partitions just sit empty while the heavy partitions remain heavy after the redistribution attempt.

Raising partition count introduces additional shuffle write overhead per partition; with 600 partitions the per-task setup cost adds up and the total stage time grows even when the skew is partially addressed by the larger task count operating across the shuffle stage of the workload.

Raising partition count requires recomputing the shuffle hash function on the larger partition space; the hash function's range changes with partition count and the keys that previously landed on the same partition may split or merge in unpredictable ways across the larger partition range.

Raising partition count works only when AQE is also enabled; without AQE the partition-count change at planning time does not propagate to the executor task allocation and the resulting stage runs at the original 200-partition distribution regardless of the configuration change.
fields.correctAnswer: Raising partition count helps when the data is uniformly distributed across keys but the per-task data is too large; with skew, the heavy keys land on whichever partitions they hash to, and the extra partitions just sit empty while the heavy partitions remain heavy after the redistribution attempt.
fields.rationale:
Partition count is about granularity, not balance. If one region holds 460K rows, those rows still hash to one (or a few) partitions even at 600 total partitions; the extra partitions hold the lighter regions and stay underutilised. The signature of skew is per-key concentration, which partition count cannot fix. Other options invent shuffle overheads, hash recomputation requirements, or AQE dependencies that are not the structural reason.

When this answer is wrong: If the slowness were due to per-task data being too large with uniform distribution (not skew), raising partition count would help directly and option A's framing would be wrong. The exercise's framing (concentrated keys) makes partition count the wrong lever.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Names shuffle write overhead; real but not the structural reason partition count fails on skew.

Option C: Invents a hash recomputation mechanism that is not how Spark's hash works.

Option D: Asserts AQE dependency for partition-count changes; not real.

fields.label: If the team chose salting, what's the trade-off compared to leaving the skew in place?
options: Salting adds a second aggregation stage to the pipeline and roughly doubles the shuffle volume (each row participates in two aggregations rather than one); the runtime improvement comes from the heavy keys being split across multiple tasks at the cost of doing the aggregation twice for every row of the input.

Salting requires manual selection of which keys to salt (the heavy ones) and which to leave unsalted; the team has to maintain a list of skewed keys that drifts as the data distribution shifts, which becomes a long-term maintenance cost across the pipeline's lifetime.

Salting introduces an additional shuffle stage in the plan; the runtime improvement from balanced partitions is partially offset by the cost of the extra shuffle, and the net benefit depends on how many heavy keys the salting actually addresses across the cluster's stage runtime measurements.

Salting changes the output column type from a flat key to a struct or array with the salt suffix; downstream consumers have to be aware of the structural change and adapt their reads accordingly to accommodate the salt suffix in the partition column structure.
fields.correctAnswer: Salting adds a second aggregation stage to the pipeline and roughly doubles the shuffle volume (each row participates in two aggregations rather than one); the runtime improvement comes from the heavy keys being split across multiple tasks at the cost of doing the aggregation twice for every row of the input.
fields.rationale:
The extra aggregation pass that salting introduces sends every row through the shuffle twice, so the total data moved through the cluster is approximately doubled. The runtime improvement comes from the heavy keys splitting across more tasks. The trade is doubled work in exchange for balanced distribution. Option B describes a real maintenance concern but smaller than the doubled-shuffle cost. Option C is partially true (the extra shuffle adds cost) but understates the structural doubling. Option D invents a column-type change that salting does not require.

When this answer is wrong: If the salting is implemented with a per-key salt cardinality (e.g., always 8 suffixes), the doubled-shuffle volume is the right framing. If implemented with a heavy-key list (rare keys not salted), option B's maintenance cost becomes more relevant. The exercise's framing (uniform salting) makes the doubled volume primary.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Names a real concern but smaller than the doubled-volume cost.

Option C: Names the extra shuffle but understates the structural doubling.

Option D: Invents a column-type change that salting does not require.

fields.label: AQE skew handling fires on skew above a configured ratio. Why might it NOT fire on this pipeline even with AQE enabled?
options: AQE skew handling requires post-shuffle data sizes to exceed the configured threshold AND the ratio between max partition size and median to exceed a configured factor; if either condition is not met, AQE does not split the partition even when the wall-clock impact is significant for the stage.

AQE skew handling applies only to join operations, not to groupBy aggregations; the spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled flag is specific to joins, and groupBy skew is not handled by the same AQE feature set even when the same skew signature is present in the histogram.

AQE skew handling requires the skew detection step to complete before the heavy partition starts processing; on this pipeline the heavy partition starts immediately at stage launch and AQE's detection window has not yet observed enough completed tasks to identify the skew.

AQE skew handling is gated by the cost-based optimiser's row-count estimates; without recent ANALYZE statistics the planner falls back to uniform distribution assumptions and AQE never triggers its skew-splitting behavior during the run.
fields.correctAnswer: AQE skew handling applies only to join operations, not to groupBy aggregations; the spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled flag is specific to joins, and groupBy skew is not handled by the same AQE feature set even when the same skew signature is present in the histogram.
fields.rationale:
spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled is, as the name says, a join-specific feature. It splits large join-side partitions at runtime. groupBy aggregations do not benefit from it; AQE does not yet have a general groupBy skew handler. The other options invent specific gating conditions (threshold AND ratio, detection window, ANALYZE dependency) that miss the structural fact that the feature is join-scoped.

When this answer is wrong: If the operation were genuinely a join, option A's gating conditions would matter and could explain a non-firing skew handler. The exercise's framing (groupBy) makes the feature simply inapplicable.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names real gating conditions but for the wrong operation; AQE skew handling does not apply to groupBy.

Option C: Invents a detection-window mechanism that does not match how AQE schedules its rules.

Option D: Asserts CBO dependency for AQE; AQE works at runtime regardless of compile-time statistics.

fields.label: The team ships salting and the stage drops to 6.5 minutes. Which observation would confirm the fix worked correctly (not just by coincidence)?
options: Total stage time at 6.5 minutes is within the team's expectations for the workload; the SLA is met with margin, the previous runs at 42 minutes are gone, and the wall-clock improvement is the primary success criterion regardless of the per-task distribution after the salting fix.

Total shuffle write volume should have approximately doubled from the original because salting adds a second aggregation pass; the doubled shuffle is the cost of salting, and observing this doubling confirms the fix is operating as designed during the cluster's stage execution.

Per-task shuffle read bytes should now show a tight distribution across all 200 tasks (e.g., 1-3 MB for every task, no outliers above 5 MB); the tight distribution is the direct evidence that the heavy keys were split across multiple tasks during the salted aggregation step.

Task duration histogram should now show a tight distribution with p50 and p99 within roughly 2x of each other; the previous 100x ratio between p50 and p99 collapses to a normal distribution, confirming the skew has been addressed and the workload now distributes evenly.
fields.correctAnswer: Per-task shuffle read bytes should now show a tight distribution across all 200 tasks (e.g., 1-3 MB for every task, no outliers above 5 MB); the tight distribution is the direct evidence that the heavy keys were split across multiple tasks during the salted aggregation step.
fields.rationale:
Look at the byte counts the tasks actually read during the shuffle. The previous 1.5 MB median vs 120 MB max imbalance should collapse to a near-uniform distribution, showing that the salted aggregation actually split the heavy keys across tasks. The duration histogram (option D) is correlated but secondary — durations can be uniform for other reasons. The SLA argument (option A) confirms the outcome but not the mechanism. Shuffle volume doubling (option B) confirms salting ran but not that it succeeded.

When this answer is wrong: If the team is doing a post-hoc justification rather than a mechanism check, the SLA argument (option A) is sufficient. The exercise's framing ('worked correctly, not just by coincidence') makes the mechanism check primary.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names SLA conformance as success; necessary but does not verify mechanism.

Option B: Verifies salting ran (doubled shuffle) but not that it succeeded (balanced output).

Option D: Verifies duration histogram balance but secondary to shuffle bytes.

tasks.title: The Stage That Spilled to Disk

description.context: A NordGrid engineer is investigating a slow shuffle stage. The Spark UI shows shuffle write at 2.1 GB, shuffle read at 2.1 GB, AND disk spill at 84 GB (forty times the shuffle volume). Total stage time is 19 minutes; executor memory is 32 GB per executor with 4 executors. The stage is the aggregation step before a final join. The team's lead asks the engineer to read the metrics and pick the right diagnosis from four candidates.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid engineer is investigating a slow shuffle stage. The Spark UI shows shuffle write at 2.1 GB, shuffle read at 2.1 GB, AND disk spill at 84 GB (forty times the shuffle volume). Total stage time is 19 minutes; executor memory is 32 GB per executor with 4 executors. The stage is the aggregation step before a final join. The team's lead asks the engineer to read the metrics and pick the right diagnosis from four candidates.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: Disk spill on the executor's local disk is shared with other Spark workloads on the cluster. The 84 GB spill is large enough to interfere with co-tenant jobs, and the team has been asked to fix the spill regardless of whether the 19-minute runtime is meeting its own SLA.

evidence.title: Platform context
evidence.content: The Customer team OWNS this pipeline. The cluster has 4 executors × 8 cores × 32 GB RAM = 128 GB total executor memory. The aggregation in the slow stage uses collect_list to gather all daily readings per meter (some meters have hundreds of readings per day after a recent sensor rollout). The Operations team OWNS the executor configuration and is the team that would change executor memory if the engineer concludes that is the right lever.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (1.2M rows after a sensor rollout that increased readings per meter from 24/day to 240/day)

evidence.label: Stage Metrics
evidence.content:
{
  "shuffle_write": "2.1 GB",
  "shuffle_read": "2.1 GB",
  "disk_spill_memory": "84 GB",
  "disk_spill_disk": "12 GB (compressed on-disk form)",
  "task_count": 200,
  "tasks_with_spill": 187,
  "p50_task_duration": "4 min",
  "p99_task_duration": "5 min"
}

evidence.title: Cluster Spec
evidence.content: 4 executors × 8 cores × 32 GB RAM each = 128 GB total executor memory

evidence.title: Aggregation Used
evidence.content: groupBy('meter_id').agg(collect_list('reading'))

evidence.label: Candidate Diagnoses
evidence.content:
[
  "Too few shuffle partitions — at 200 partitions, each task processes ~10 MB of shuffle input but accumulates a much larger collect_list buffer in memory",
  "Too many shuffle partitions — at 200 partitions, the per-task overhead exceeds the per-task work, and the spill is unrelated to partition count",
  "Broadcast side too large — a broadcast join above this stage pushed memory pressure into the aggregation, causing the spill",
  "Executor memory mis-tuned — the per-task memory budget (~1 GB after overhead) is smaller than the per-task collect_list buffer, forcing every task to spill"
]

fields.label: What does the 40:1 ratio between disk spill and shuffle volume tell you?
options: The aggregation is accumulating much more data in memory than it ultimately emits; collect_list materialises every input row's value into an in-memory buffer before producing the per-key output, and the buffer size dominates the per-task memory footprint during the stage's execution.

The shuffle is reading the same data multiple times because the disk spill creates additional read passes; each spill-and-restore cycle adds the spilled volume back into the shuffle read counter, which inflates the ratio observed in the Spark UI for the stage.

The shuffle is using a compressed format that decompresses to much larger data in memory; the 2.1 GB shuffle write decompresses to roughly 84 GB during the in-memory phase of the aggregation, matching the spill volume observed during the run.

The spill is leaking across stages because Spark is not freeing the previous stage's spill buffers; the 84 GB spill is the accumulated total across multiple stages of the pipeline and not the per-stage spill from the aggregation alone in this Spark UI view.
fields.correctAnswer: The aggregation is accumulating much more data in memory than it ultimately emits; collect_list materialises every input row's value into an in-memory buffer before producing the per-key output, and the buffer size dominates the per-task memory footprint during the stage's execution.
fields.rationale:
The 40-to-1 ratio between memory pressure and on-shuffle volume tells you the operator is holding much more data inside the task than what the task hands off. collect_list materialises every input row's value into a buffer before producing the per-key output. With 240 readings per meter and 1.2M meters, the per-task buffer holds many times the shuffle-side volume before it produces the per-key output. The buffer-vs-output asymmetry is the structural cause. Other options invent specific mechanisms (re-reads, decompression expansion, leaked spill) that are not how Spark's spill counters work.

When this answer is wrong: If the aggregation were a scalar function (sum, count, avg), the buffer would be small and the 40:1 ratio would not arise. The exercise's framing (collect_list) makes the buffer the dominant memory user.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Invents a re-read inflation of the shuffle counter; not how spill metrics work.

Option C: Invents a compression expansion factor of 40x; compression ratios are typically 3-10x.

Option D: Invents a cross-stage leak; spill is per-stage in the Spark UI view.

fields.label: Which of the four candidate diagnoses fits the metrics?
options: Too few shuffle partitions is the right diagnosis; raising partitions from 200 to a higher count would distribute the work across more tasks and reduce per-task memory pressure, eliminating the spill on the per-task aggregation buffer.

Too many shuffle partitions is the right diagnosis; the per-task overhead at 200 partitions is what shows up as the 19-minute runtime, and the spill is a side-effect of the small per-task work that triggers the executor's memory manager more frequently than it should.

Broadcast side too large is the right diagnosis; the broadcast join above the aggregation occupies executor memory that the aggregation needs, and the spill happens because the broadcast crowds out the aggregation's buffer in the executor memory pool.

Executor memory mis-tuned is the right diagnosis; the per-task memory budget is too small for the collect_list buffer's size, and the fix is to raise executor memory (or lower the parallelism per executor) so each task has enough memory to hold its buffer.
fields.correctAnswer: Executor memory mis-tuned is the right diagnosis; the per-task memory budget is too small for the collect_list buffer's size, and the fix is to raise executor memory (or lower the parallelism per executor) so each task has enough memory to hold its buffer.
fields.rationale:
187 of 200 tasks spill — the problem is per-task. Per-task memory budget is roughly (executor memory × memory fraction) / cores ≈ 32 × 0.6 / 8 ≈ 2.4 GB minus overhead ≈ 1 GB. With 240 readings per meter and meter_ids distributed across tasks, each task's collect_list buffer exceeds 1 GB and spills. The fix is to raise the per-task memory budget. Other options pick partition count (covered in next question), broadcast pressure (the plan does not show a broadcast above), or invert the partition-count logic.

When this answer is wrong: If only a few tasks spilled (say, 5 of 200), the cause would be skew rather than a budget mis-tune and option C's broadcast diagnosis or a different concentrated-pressure diagnosis would apply. The exercise's framing (187/200 tasks spilling) makes the budget the structural issue.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Picks partition count as the budget lever; partitions do not change per-task memory.

Option B: Inverts partition-count effect; more partitions reduce per-task work, not increase it.

Option C: Invents broadcast pressure that the plan does not show.

fields.label: Why is 'too few shuffle partitions' not the right answer here?
options: Raising partition count proportionally reduces per-task data size; 200 → 600 partitions would cut the per-task buffer to a third of its current size, which is the expected behavior for a collect_list aggregation under the cluster's parallelism configuration.

Partition count helps when the per-task work is too large but the data is uniformly distributed; with 187 of 200 tasks spilling, the issue is per-task budget not partition granularity, and raising partitions does not change the executor memory available per task.

Raising partition count would help only if the AQE coalesce-shuffle-partitions feature is disabled; AQE counters partition-count changes by collapsing partitions back to a runtime-appropriate count, so the partition raise would not survive the AQE pass on the cluster.

Partition count is independent of memory pressure because Spark allocates memory per executor, not per partition; the partition count change does not affect the per-task memory budget and the spill would happen at the same rate after the change as before.
fields.correctAnswer: Partition count helps when the per-task work is too large but the data is uniformly distributed; with 187 of 200 tasks spilling, the issue is per-task budget not partition granularity, and raising partitions does not change the executor memory available per task.
fields.rationale:
Partition count and per-task memory budget are independent levers. Adding partitions reduces per-task data volume going into the shuffle, but each task still gets the same memory budget. If the aggregation buffer needs more than that budget, more partitions does not help. The other options invent specific cross-interactions (proportional reduction without limits, AQE counter-action, memory-allocation independence) that miss the proportionality structure.

When this answer is wrong: If the buffer were proportional to the partition's row count (a different aggregation pattern), raising partitions would help directly. The exercise's framing (collect_list per key, not per partition) keeps the per-task budget the binding constraint.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Asserts partition count proportionally reduces buffer; only true for per-partition (not per-key) aggregations.

Option C: Invokes AQE coalesce; would matter for the runtime but not for the budget question.

Option D: Asserts memory is per-executor and independent of partitions; partially true but conflates allocation with usage.

fields.label: If the engineer raises executor memory from 32 GB to 64 GB, what's the expected change?
options: The spill volume would drop to roughly half, since the per-task memory budget doubles (from ~1 GB to ~2 GB) but the per-task collect_list buffer averages larger than 2 GB; some tasks still spill but the total volume is reduced proportionally to the memory increase across the cluster.

The spill volume would drop to near zero, since the doubled per-task memory budget (~1 GB → ~2 GB) would now hold most per-task collect_list buffers without spilling; the few tasks that still spill would be the largest meters (the ones with hundreds of readings per day).

The spill volume would not change because Spark's executor memory tuning is not the binding constraint here; the spill comes from the executor's serializer buffer rather than the aggregation buffer, and the serializer buffer is sized by a different configuration setting on the cluster.

The spill volume would drop to near zero AND runtime would drop substantially; the aggregation runs in memory without spill cycles, and the 19-minute stage runtime collapses to the underlying CPU-bound aggregate time (a few minutes) once the memory pressure is removed.
fields.correctAnswer: The spill volume would drop to near zero AND runtime would drop substantially; the aggregation runs in memory without spill cycles, and the 19-minute stage runtime collapses to the underlying CPU-bound aggregate time (a few minutes) once the memory pressure is removed.
fields.rationale:
Raising executor memory doubles the per-task budget. For a workload where the per-task buffer is sized between 1 and 2 GB, doubling the budget to roughly 2 GB removes the spill for most tasks. The stage runtime then drops to the CPU-bound aggregation time, which is a few minutes. Options A and B disagree about partial vs full elimination; the metrics suggest near-zero spill is achievable. Option C invents a different spill source.

When this answer is wrong: If the per-task buffer for a few large meters exceeded 2 GB even after the memory raise, option B's partial-spill answer would describe the outcome. The exercise's framing (typical readings volume) suggests 2 GB is enough.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Picks partial reduction; underestimates the memory effect.

Option B: Picks near-zero spill without noting the runtime drop that accompanies it.

Option C: Invents serializer-buffer source for the spill; the workload's buffer is the aggregation.

fields.label: An alternative to raising executor memory is to change the aggregation. Which alternative would address the spill at its source?
options: Replace collect_list with collect_set; the set deduplicates entries and the result fits in less memory than the list, which is enough to bring the per-task buffer under the available memory and eliminate the spill across the affected tasks.

Replace collect_list with sum or count; the scalar aggregate occupies a fixed small amount of memory per group (a single accumulator) rather than a buffer that grows with the per-group row count, eliminating the spill regardless of executor memory configuration.

Replace the groupBy with a window function partitioned by meter_id; the window function operates on a sliding range rather than collecting all rows into memory, and the resulting computation does not need to materialise the per-meter list at any single task.

Replace the groupBy with a join to a pre-aggregated table; the join eliminates the aggregation entirely and the collect_list operation never runs against the raw data, removing the spill at its source by removing the operation that caused it.
fields.correctAnswer: Replace collect_list with sum or count; the scalar aggregate occupies a fixed small amount of memory per group (a single accumulator) rather than a buffer that grows with the per-group row count, eliminating the spill regardless of executor memory configuration.
fields.rationale:
The structural cause of the spill is a buffer that scales with how many rows fall under each key; swapping the aggregation for a scalar accumulator (sum, count, avg) removes that scaling entirely. The buffer becomes a fixed-size accumulator. If the downstream pipeline truly needs the list, this change is not viable; but if a scalar summary is sufficient, this is the cleanest fix. collect_set (option A) helps if there are many duplicates but still builds a buffer. Window functions (option C) operate row-by-row but the per-meter materialisation cost depends on the function. Pre-aggregation (option D) is a different architectural change.

When this answer is wrong: If the downstream pipeline genuinely needs the full list of readings per meter (e.g., for a custom serialisation step), the scalar replacement does not preserve semantics and option A's collect_set might be a partial mitigation. The exercise's framing (asking what addresses spill at source) makes the scalar replacement the cleanest answer when feasible.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Picks collect_set; still builds an in-memory buffer, just smaller.

Option C: Picks window functions as a row-by-row alternative; depends on the function whether it materialises per-key data.

Option D: Picks pre-aggregation; architectural change rather than a fix to the operation itself.
