tasks.title: AQE On, AQE Off — Which Plan Wins?

description.context: A NordGrid analytics engineer runs the same query twice, once with AQE disabled and once with AQE enabled. The compiled plans are identical at submit time. The runtime plans differ. The team's lead asks the engineer to read both runtime plans and identify which AQE feature (coalesce-shuffle-partitions, broadcast conversion, or skew handling) was responsible for each visible change.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid analytics engineer runs the same query twice, once with AQE disabled and once with AQE enabled. The compiled plans are identical at submit time. The runtime plans differ. The team's lead asks the engineer to read both runtime plans and identify which AQE feature (coalesce-shuffle-partitions, broadcast conversion, or skew handling) was responsible for each visible change.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: AQE is currently enabled cluster-wide by the Platform team's default configuration. A few teams have disabled it in their own session configurations citing 'unpredictable plan behaviour'. The Analytics team is the one running this query and wants to understand exactly what AQE is doing for them before deciding whether to keep the default.

evidence.title: Platform context
evidence.content: The Customer team OWNS the meters table. The Billing team OWNS a customer_tier reference table (~3 MB). The Substations team OWNS the substations table (~49 MB). The query joins all three and aggregates by region. AQE features at issue: coalesce-shuffle-partitions, broadcast conversion, skew handling.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (1.2M rows), customer_tier (3 MB), substations.csv (49 MB)

evidence.label: Query
evidence.content:
(meters
    .filter(col('date') == '2026-05-10')
    .join(customer_tier, 'customer_id', 'left')
    .join(substations, 'substation_id', 'left')
    .groupBy('region')
    .agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total_kw')))

evidence.label: Runtime Plan Aqe Off
evidence.content:
Stages: 5
- Exchange after meters scan (200 partitions)
- SortMergeJoin meters × customer_tier (200 partitions each side)
- SortMergeJoin (intermediate) × substations (200 partitions each side)
- Exchange before final HashAggregate (200 partitions)
- Final HashAggregate (200 output partitions, 12 non-empty)
Total runtime: 14 min

evidence.label: Runtime Plan Aqe On
evidence.content:
Stages: 5
- Exchange after meters scan (200 partitions)
- BroadcastHashJoin meters × customer_tier (AQE converted from SortMergeJoin; post-shuffle size 3 MB < 10 MB threshold)
- SortMergeJoin (intermediate) × substations (still SortMergeJoin; substations 49 MB > 10 MB threshold)
- Exchange before final HashAggregate (coalesced to 12 partitions, AQE coalesce-shuffle-partitions)
- Final HashAggregate (12 output partitions, all non-empty)
Total runtime: 4 min

fields.label: Which AQE feature converted the customer_tier join from SortMergeJoin to BroadcastHashJoin?
options: Coalesce-shuffle-partitions converted the join by reducing partition count to match the small customer_tier table; the smaller partition count on the join's build side made it eligible for a broadcast under the configured threshold across the cluster's runtime plan.

Skew handling converted the join because the customer_id distribution was skewed; AQE split the heavy keys and the resulting smaller partitions per key triggered the broadcast-conversion path indirectly through the skew-handling stage.

Statistics propagation converted the join by inferring the post-filter row count on the meters side; the inferred count was used to reassess the broadcast eligibility check against the customer_tier table's size during the query's execution.

Broadcast conversion (spark.sql.adaptive.localShuffleReader.enabled and spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold) converted the join after observing the actual post-shuffle size of customer_tier at 3 MB, which fell below the 10 MB threshold and triggered the conversion at the stage boundary.
fields.correctAnswer: Broadcast conversion (spark.sql.adaptive.localShuffleReader.enabled and spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold) converted the join after observing the actual post-shuffle size of customer_tier at 3 MB, which fell below the 10 MB threshold and triggered the conversion at the stage boundary.
fields.rationale:
Broadcast conversion is the AQE feature that converts SortMergeJoin to BroadcastHashJoin at a stage boundary based on observed post-shuffle data size. The runtime plan annotation 'AQE converted from SortMergeJoin; post-shuffle size 3 MB < 10 MB threshold' names the feature explicitly. The other options assign credit to wrong features (coalesce, skew handling, statistics propagation) that operate on different aspects of the plan.

When this answer is wrong: If the customer_tier table had been below 10 MB at compile time (with ANALYZE statistics), the broadcast would have been picked at planning rather than at runtime by AQE. The exercise's framing (AQE conversion at the stage boundary) places the conversion at runtime.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Conflates coalesce (partition count) with broadcast conversion (join strategy).

Option B: Conflates skew handling with broadcast conversion.

Option C: Names statistics propagation; AQE uses runtime sizes, not propagated estimates.

fields.label: Why did AQE NOT convert the substations join from SortMergeJoin to BroadcastHashJoin?
options: The substations table at 49 MB exceeds the AQE broadcast threshold (10 MB default); AQE evaluates post-shuffle size against the threshold at each stage boundary and 49 MB exceeds the threshold so the conversion does not fire on the substations join.

AQE applies broadcast conversion only once per query and the customer_tier conversion consumed the conversion budget; the second join is left as SortMergeJoin because AQE's per-query conversion limit is set to one in the default configuration on the cluster.

Broadcasting two tables in the same query is structurally complex because both broadcasts compete for executor memory; AQE picks the smaller table for broadcast and leaves the larger one as SortMergeJoin even when both sides are individually broadcast-eligible at their respective threshold.

AQE's broadcast conversion is disabled by default for joins above a certain depth in the plan; the substations join is the second join in the chain and falls below the depth threshold AQE uses to limit its conversion scope for predictability of behavior.
fields.correctAnswer: The substations table at 49 MB exceeds the AQE broadcast threshold (10 MB default); AQE evaluates post-shuffle size against the threshold at each stage boundary and 49 MB exceeds the threshold so the conversion does not fire on the substations join.
fields.rationale:
AQE's broadcast threshold check compares post-shuffle size to the configured threshold. The substations table at 49 MB exceeds the 10 MB threshold, so the conversion does not fire. The runtime plan annotation 'still SortMergeJoin; substations 49 MB > 10 MB threshold' names this directly. Other options invent specific gating mechanisms (per-query conversion limit, two-broadcast complexity, plan-depth threshold) that AQE does not actually use.

When this answer is wrong: If the team had raised spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold to 64 MB, the substations join would also have converted. The exercise's framing (default 10 MB threshold) keeps substations out of broadcast range.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Invents a per-query conversion budget; AQE has no such limit.

Option C: Invents a 'two broadcasts compete' mechanism; broadcasts in the same query are independent.

Option D: Invents a plan-depth threshold for AQE; not a real configuration.

fields.label: Which AQE feature reduced the final aggregate's partition count from 200 to 12?
options: Broadcast conversion reduced the partition count by collapsing the post-aggregate partitions into a smaller set after observing that the per-partition data was small; the conversion fired indirectly on the aggregate's output to match the downstream consumer's expected file count.

Skew handling reduced the partition count by detecting that 188 of 200 partitions were empty; the heavy partitions (the 12 non-empty ones) were preserved and the empty ones were collapsed into a single follow-up partition for cleanup.

Coalesce-shuffle-partitions (spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled) reduced the partition count by inspecting the post-shuffle data sizes; with only 12 non-empty partitions out of 200, AQE coalesced them down to 12 to match the actual workload.

Statistics propagation reduced the partition count by computing the post-aggregate cardinality from the upstream statistics; the inferred 12-region cardinality propagated to the shuffle partition count at query compilation time before any stage ran.
fields.correctAnswer: Coalesce-shuffle-partitions (spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled) reduced the partition count by inspecting the post-shuffle data sizes; with only 12 non-empty partitions out of 200, AQE coalesced them down to 12 to match the actual workload.
fields.rationale:
Coalesce-shuffle-partitions (spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled) reduces partition count post-shuffle based on observed data sizes. With 12 regions and 200 shuffle partitions, 188 partitions are empty; AQE coalesces the 12 non-empty ones down to a tight partition count matching the actual data. The runtime plan annotation 'coalesced to 12 partitions, AQE coalesce-shuffle-partitions' names the feature directly. Other options assign credit to wrong features.

When this answer is wrong: If the workload had been larger (12 regions with substantial data per region), AQE might coalesce to a different count based on the per-partition target size. The exercise's framing (12 small per-region totals) makes the coalesce target match the row count.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Reassigns broadcast conversion to a partition-count role.

Option B: Reassigns skew handling to empty-partition collapsing.

Option D: Names statistics propagation; AQE uses runtime sizes, not compile-time estimates.

fields.label: If the engineer disables only the broadcast conversion feature (keeping coalesce and skew handling), what changes?
options: The customer_tier join stays as SortMergeJoin, but the final aggregate still coalesces to 12 partitions; the runtime would land between 4 and 14 minutes because the broadcast conversion was contributing the larger share of the saving on this query.

The customer_tier join stays as SortMergeJoin AND the final aggregate stays at 200 partitions; the two features are coupled in the AQE configuration and disabling broadcast conversion also disables the coalesce behavior at the stage boundary in the same plan.

The customer_tier join stays as SortMergeJoin AND the substations join would have been converted to broadcast if it had been eligible; coalesce-shuffle-partitions takes over as the dominant feature when broadcast conversion is disabled in the cluster's configuration.

Nothing changes in the runtime plan; the broadcast conversion feature is logically dependent on the coalesce feature and disabling one disables the other through the AQE configuration's dependency chain in the cluster's runtime planner.
fields.correctAnswer: The customer_tier join stays as SortMergeJoin AND the final aggregate stays at 200 partitions; the two features are coupled in the AQE configuration and disabling broadcast conversion also disables the coalesce behavior at the stage boundary in the same plan.
fields.rationale:
AQE's features are independently configurable. Disabling broadcast conversion preserves coalesce-shuffle-partitions and skew handling. The customer_tier join stays as SortMergeJoin (no broadcast conversion fires) but the final aggregate still coalesces to 12 partitions. Runtime would be intermediate between 14 and 4 minutes — the coalesce saves on the aggregate stage, the broadcast conversion would have saved on the join. Options B and D claim the features are coupled, which is false. Option C invents substations broadcast eligibility.

When this answer is wrong: If the AQE configuration in the specific Spark version coupled the features (e.g., a future release), option B's framing would describe the actual outcome. The exercise's framing (current Spark with independent flags) makes the independence the right answer.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: (see explanation)

Option C: Invents substations broadcast eligibility that the exercise has ruled out at 49 MB.

Option D: Asserts feature dependency; not how AQE flags are organised.

fields.label: The team is debating whether to leave AQE on by default. Which argument is the strongest in favor?
options: AQE adapts to runtime data sizes without requiring the team to run ANALYZE on every table or to maintain partition-count tuning per query; the operational simplicity of relying on AQE outweighs the small predictability cost of plans that vary by run on the same query.

AQE produces runtime plans that match or improve compile-time plans in most cases; the rare cases where AQE produces a worse plan are recoverable by disabling AQE for the specific query, while the common cases where AQE improves the plan benefit from the default-on setting.

AQE is the only path to broadcast conversion for tables whose size becomes visible only at runtime (post-filter, post-aggregate); without AQE these conversions cannot happen automatically and the team would have to maintain manual broadcast hints across every query that joins these tables.

AQE's coalesce-shuffle-partitions feature directly addresses the 'too many empty partitions' problem that the default 200-partition setting produces for small workloads; the feature is structurally needed because the global default cannot be both correct for small workloads and correct for large ones at the same time.
fields.correctAnswer: AQE adapts to runtime data sizes without requiring the team to run ANALYZE on every table or to maintain partition-count tuning per query; the operational simplicity of relying on AQE outweighs the small predictability cost of plans that vary by run on the same query.
fields.rationale:
Operational simplicity is the strongest argument. AQE adapts to runtime conditions without requiring per-query ANALYZE schedules, per-query partition tuning, or per-query hints. The cost is that plans vary by run, which some teams find unpredictable, but the operational saving across the cluster is large. Other options name real benefits (option B's 'matches or improves', option C's runtime-only conversions, option D's coalesce-specific saving) but each is a narrower argument than the overall operational simplicity.

When this answer is wrong: If the team's primary concern is plan predictability for regulated workloads (e.g., the Billing team's auditor wants identical plans every run), option B's 'most cases match or improve' becomes the right framing because it acknowledges the predictability cost. The exercise's framing (operational simplicity argument) leads with the broader benefit.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Names a narrower argument (per-query recovery) rather than the structural benefit.

Option C: Names a specific feature (broadcast conversion) as the structural benefit.

Option D: Names a specific feature (coalesce) as the structural benefit.

tasks.title: The Broadcast Threshold That Halved the Runtime

description.context: A NordGrid engineer raises spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold from the default 10 MB to 50 MB on the daily Silver pipeline. The pipeline runtime drops from 26 minutes to 13 minutes. The lead asks the engineer to identify three OTHER configuration changes that could have produced the same outcome through different mechanisms, and to explain when each alternative would or would not be the right choice.
description.task: Read the artifact and answer the recognition questions below.

evidence.title: Scenario
evidence.content: A NordGrid engineer raises spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold from the default 10 MB to 50 MB on the daily Silver pipeline. The pipeline runtime drops from 26 minutes to 13 minutes. The lead asks the engineer to identify three OTHER configuration changes that could have produced the same outcome through different mechanisms, and to explain when each alternative would or would not be the right choice.

evidence.title: Production constraint
evidence.content: The runtime saving is real. The team is auditing the change for portability across other pipelines and across Spark version upgrades. The engineer needs to know whether the change is durable or whether it depends on specific cluster state that might change.

evidence.title: Platform context
evidence.content: The Customer team OWNS this pipeline. The cluster is shared with three other teams whose pipelines also join against various reference tables. The change to autoBroadcastJoinThreshold is currently scoped to the team's job-level configuration (spark.conf.set). The Operations team OWNS the cluster's default configurations.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: meters.csv (1.2M rows), tariff_history.csv (42 MB; the reference table being joined that fell under the new threshold)

evidence.title: The Change
evidence.content: spark.conf.set('spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold', 50 * 1024 * 1024)  # 50 MB

evidence.label: Before After
Candidate Alternatives
evidence.content:
[
  "Run ANALYZE TABLE on tariff_history (the table was 42 MB but the catalog held the 8 EiB fallback)",
  "Add a broadcast(tariff_history) hint to the query",
  "Enable AQE (the post-shuffle size of tariff_history after the date filter on meters could fall below the original 10 MB threshold)",
  "Pre-filter tariff_history to the active rows only (the filter reduces the table to ~6 MB)"
]

fields.label: Which alternative achieves the same broadcast strategy via the SAME mechanism (cost-based optimizer picks broadcast based on size)?
options: Adding broadcast(tariff_history) hint achieves it via the same mechanism because the hint feeds the planner the same broadcast-eligibility decision it would have reached on its own with a different threshold setting on the cluster's job configuration.

Running ANALYZE on tariff_history achieves it via the same mechanism: the catalog now holds 42 MB instead of 8 EiB and the planner reads 42 MB at compile time. The size falls under the raised or default threshold that the planner uses to decide broadcast eligibility for the join in question.

Enabling AQE achieves it via the same mechanism because AQE's broadcast conversion uses the same cost-based optimization framework that the compile-time planner uses; the only difference is the timing of the decision across the query's execution lifecycle.

Pre-filtering tariff_history achieves it via the same mechanism because the filter produces a smaller in-memory representation that the planner reads as the input to its broadcast decision step on the query's execution plan.
fields.correctAnswer: Running ANALYZE on tariff_history achieves it via the same mechanism: the catalog now holds 42 MB instead of 8 EiB and the planner reads 42 MB at compile time. The size falls under the raised or default threshold that the planner uses to decide broadcast eligibility for the join in question.
fields.rationale:
ANALYZE updates the catalog from the 8 EiB fallback to the real 42 MB. The planner then reads 42 MB at compile time. With the default 10 MB threshold this still fails (42 > 10), but if the team raised the threshold to 50 MB it would succeed. The mechanism — cost-based optimizer reading size from catalog and comparing to threshold — is the same as before. The other options describe different mechanisms (hint override, AQE runtime decision, data shape change).

When this answer is wrong: If the team's setup includes ANALYZE in the job's startup hooks, the catalog-based mechanism is already in use and the question would be about which approach to retire. The exercise's framing (raising threshold vs running ANALYZE) treats both as alternatives.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats hints as a same-mechanism alternative; hints override, they do not influence.

Option C: Treats AQE as same-mechanism; AQE's runtime decision is structurally different.

Option D: Treats pre-filter as same-mechanism; the filter changes the input, not the decision step.

fields.label: Which alternative achieves the broadcast via a DIFFERENT mechanism (overriding the planner's decision rather than influencing it)?
options: Running ANALYZE achieves the broadcast via a different mechanism because the statistics refresh bypasses the cost-based optimization and gives the planner a direct override on the join strategy through the catalog metadata update step.

Enabling AQE achieves the broadcast via a different mechanism because AQE replaces the planner's decision with its own runtime decision; the cost-based optimizer's strategy is overridden by the AQE rule that converts joins at stage boundaries.

Adding broadcast(tariff_history) hint achieves it via a different mechanism because the hint is a directive that overrides the planner's size-based decision; the planner picks broadcast regardless of what the threshold would have decided based on the catalog statistics value.

Pre-filtering achieves it via a different mechanism because the filter changes the input data shape; the planner sees a different table than it would have seen and the resulting broadcast decision is technically against a different table, not the original tariff_history.
fields.correctAnswer: Adding broadcast(tariff_history) hint achieves it via a different mechanism because the hint is a directive that overrides the planner's size-based decision; the planner picks broadcast regardless of what the threshold would have decided based on the catalog statistics value.
fields.rationale:
Hints are directives. The planner is told to use BroadcastHashJoin regardless of what the cost-based optimizer would have decided. The other options either describe same-mechanism alternatives (ANALYZE, pre-filter both feed the planner different inputs but the planner still makes the decision) or describe a different timing (AQE's runtime decision still goes through cost-based logic, just at a different time).

When this answer is wrong: If the team uses noBroadcast hints elsewhere (which also override the planner), both directions of hint use would be same-mechanism overrides and the question would be moot. The exercise's framing (raising threshold which is a parameter, vs hint which is a directive) makes the override the cleanest 'different mechanism'.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats ANALYZE as bypassing the optimizer; ANALYZE updates inputs, the optimizer still decides.

Option B: Treats AQE as overriding rather than re-deciding; AQE re-decides at runtime using the same logic.

Option D: Treats pre-filter as changing the table identity; the planner sees the filtered DataFrame, not a different table.

fields.label: If the team's engineer is auditing the change for portability across Spark version upgrades, which alternative is most likely to keep working without revisiting?
options: Running ANALYZE keeps working because the statistics format and the planner's use of statistics are stable across Spark releases; the catalog-recorded size is the input the planner reads, and the stability of the input is what makes the alternative durable across upgrades.

Raising the threshold keeps working because the configuration is a numeric setting that Spark respects across upgrades; the value is portable and applies the same way to any future Spark version's broadcast eligibility decision step in the planner.

Enabling AQE keeps working because AQE is a deliberately portable framework that takes responsibility for runtime decisions; the team does not have to manage broadcast eligibility manually and AQE handles upgrades transparently from the team's perspective.

Adding a broadcast hint keeps working because hints are a documented part of the SQL interface that Spark respects across upgrades; the team's intent is explicit in the query and survives changes to the planner's internal decision-making behavior.
fields.correctAnswer: Running ANALYZE keeps working because the statistics format and the planner's use of statistics are stable across Spark releases; the catalog-recorded size is the input the planner reads, and the stability of the input is what makes the alternative durable across upgrades.
fields.rationale:
Catalog statistics survive Spark version upgrades better than almost anything else; the format Spark records them in and the way the planner reads them are stable interfaces. The other options have version-dependent behavior: thresholds get new defaults, AQE features change between major versions, hint syntax has evolved. ANALYZE is the boring, durable option — the planner reads catalog statistics the same way across versions even when the surrounding behavior changes.

When this answer is wrong: If the table is too small for ANALYZE to be worth scheduling (e.g., a one-off reference table), the threshold raise is simpler and arguably equally portable for that case. The exercise's framing (auditing for portability) makes the catalog-stability argument the strongest.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Asserts threshold portability; defaults and bounds change across versions.

Option C: Asserts AQE is portable across upgrades; AQE features are actively evolving.

Option D: Asserts hint portability; hint syntax has changed across major versions.

fields.label: The team is concerned that raising the threshold to 50 MB might cause problems on OTHER queries. Which scenario would surface the issue most clearly?
options: A query that joins meters to a 45 MB reference table on an executor with only 8 GB of memory; the broadcast of 45 MB to each executor consumes a meaningful fraction of the per-executor budget, leaving less memory for the rest of the join's working set.

A query that joins meters to the same tariff_history table but with a slightly different filter that returns more data; the post-filter size could exceed 50 MB and the broadcast would fail at runtime with a too-large-broadcast error on the cluster.

A query that runs against a different cluster with a smaller driver process; the broadcast operation runs through the driver and a 50 MB broadcast against a 2 GB driver could OOM the driver during the broadcast collection step.

A query that joins meters to a chain of three reference tables of about 30 MB each; all three would broadcast at the 50 MB threshold, the executor memory holds 90 MB of broadcast state, and the per-executor memory pressure compounds across the three broadcasts.
fields.correctAnswer: A query that joins meters to a chain of three reference tables of about 30 MB each; all three would broadcast at the 50 MB threshold, the executor memory holds 90 MB of broadcast state, and the per-executor memory pressure compounds across the three broadcasts.
fields.rationale:
The compounding effect across multiple broadcasts is the structural risk. A single 30 MB broadcast under a 50 MB threshold is fine in isolation. Three 30 MB broadcasts in the same query stack on the executor memory and the 90 MB combined sits under no single threshold check. This is the failure mode the threshold raise opens up. Other options describe single-broadcast risks (option A's per-executor memory, option B's runtime size, option C's driver memory) but the multi-broadcast scenario is the clearest demonstration of the threshold raise's portability risk.

When this answer is wrong: If the team's queries never join multiple reference tables in the same query, the compounding risk is theoretical and option A's single-broadcast memory pressure becomes the practical concern. The exercise's framing (auditing for portability) makes the multi-broadcast scenario the structural risk.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Picks single-broadcast memory pressure; real but smaller than compounding risk.

Option B: Picks too-large-broadcast error; would happen at 50 MB threshold for tables that grow past 50 MB.

Option C: Picks driver OOM; specific to driver sizing, not a portability concern across the cluster.

fields.label: The team is choosing between the threshold raise and ANALYZE as the durable fix. Which factor most strongly favors ANALYZE?
options: ANALYZE is durable because it touches only the table in question; the threshold raise applies globally to every join the team's job runs, while ANALYZE leaves the threshold alone and updates one table's catalog entry to a correct value across the cluster.

ANALYZE is durable because it is a self-correcting mechanism; if the table grows beyond the broadcast threshold in the future, the next ANALYZE run reflects the new size and the planner switches back to SortMergeJoin automatically without team intervention.

ANALYZE is durable because it gives the planner accurate input at compile time; the threshold raise compensates for missing statistics by relaxing the safety check, while ANALYZE eliminates the missing-statistics condition that motivated the relaxation in the first place.

ANALYZE is durable because it is a one-time cost; once the statistics are recorded the catalog holds them indefinitely, while the threshold raise requires the team to remember the configuration on every cluster restart and every team-member onboarding into the codebase.
fields.correctAnswer: ANALYZE is durable because it gives the planner accurate input at compile time; the threshold raise compensates for missing statistics by relaxing the safety check, while ANALYZE eliminates the missing-statistics condition that motivated the relaxation in the first place.
fields.rationale:
ANALYZE addresses the cause; the threshold-raise only works around the symptom. With real statistics, the planner makes the right decision under the default threshold. This is structurally cleaner because it does not relax the safety check for all other joins. Other options name real benefits (table-scoped, self-correcting, one-time) but each is narrower than the structural argument that ANALYZE eliminates the underlying condition rather than working around it.

When this answer is wrong: If the team's table grows past the threshold in a few months and the ANALYZE schedule does not capture the growth, the self-correcting argument (option B) becomes the most relevant. The exercise's framing (durable fix) makes the structural argument the strongest.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Names table-scope as the structural argument; true but narrower than the cause-vs-symptom framing.

Option B: Names self-correction; relies on a maintained ANALYZE schedule.

Option D: Names one-time cost; threshold-raise is also one-time once configured.
